docs.title: Helpers PS
docs.text:
Internal library of the Portfolio Solutions team for financial analysis, institutional charts and report production. It turns a pandas DataFrame into a standardized chart, a styled table image, a PowerPoint slide or an Excel sheet, with the same look and feel everywhere.

import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()
g = hp.GraphMtplt(prices).graph_line().add_title("Equity indices").add_legend()

docs.title: What is inside
docs.text:
Component Access What it does Documentation GraphMtplt hp.GraphMtplt Matplotlib charts in the institutional style: line, bar, pie, box & whiskers and distribution, with tags, dots, shaded regions, reference lines and Bloomberg-style axes. GraphMtplt Calcs hp.Calcs Financial calculations over price DataFrames: YTD / MTD, volatility, Sharpe, drawdown, beta, tracking error, capture ratios, VaR, technical indicators... Calcs DfStyling hp.DfStyling Turns tables (and charts) into one presentation-ready image: styled DataFrames on a grid with titles, notes and sources. DfStyling Ppt hp.Ppt Native, editable PowerPoint charts (line, bar, pie, bubble, waterfall) and template helpers to fill texts and tables. Ppt Excel hp.Excel Write DataFrames to open or closed workbooks, optionally as Excel tables or with styles. Excel

Other public objects: hp.set_graph_theme (global chart theme), hp.PALETA_COLORES (institutional color palette) and hp.__version__.

docs.title: A typical workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Prices<br/>DataFrame] --> B[Calcs<br/>metrics]
    B --> C[GraphMtplt<br/>charts]
    B --> D[DfStyling<br/>tables]
    C --> E[Ppt<br/>slides]
    D --> E
    B --> F[Excel<br/>workbooks]
  1. Calculate the metrics with hp.Calcs (returns a Series / DataFrame).
  2. Chart them with hp.GraphMtplt (a PNG buffer) and format the tables with hp.DfStyling (an image).
  3. Deliver in a deck with hp.Ppt (native charts, or the pictures from step 2) and / or in hp.Excel.

The same data layout runs through the whole package: a DataFrame whose index is the date (or category) and whose columns are the series.

docs.title: Conventions used in this documentation
docs.text:
• Code blocks are complete: copy and paste them in order and they run. Each page starts with the sample data it needs (generated with numpy, so no files are required).
  • hp is always import helpers_ps as hp.
  • Images are produced by the code shown next to them.
  • Argument tables list the default value of every parameter.
  • Methods of GraphMtplt and TableSheet return the object, so calls are chained between parentheses.

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text:
pip install helpers_ps@git+https://github.com/jc-ocampob/helpers_ps.git@v0.3.3

Replace v0.3.3 with the tag (or branch) you want. Without a tag the default branch is installed:

pip install helpers_ps@git+https://github.com/jc-ocampob/helpers_ps.git

To upgrade an existing installation:

pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall --no-deps helpers_ps@git+https://github.com/jc-ocampob/helpers_ps.git@v0.3.3

Check the version:

import helpers_ps as hp

hp.__version__

Requirements

Python 3.10 or newer (3.11 is used to build this documentation). The main dependencies (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, adjustText, scipy, seaborn, plotly, python-pptx, xlsxwriter, xlwings, xbbg, and pywin32 on Windows) are installed automatically.

docs.title: Extra requirements by component
docs.text: Component Extra requirement DfStyling (TableSheet) A headless browser through Playwright: pip install playwright, then either have Chrome / Edge installed (used automatically) or run python -m playwright install chromium. Excel (to_excel_open) Microsoft Excel installed (Windows / macOS) and xlwings. Bbg A Bloomberg Terminal session on the machine (not documented yet). Fonts The default font is Inter. Install it in the operating system (and restart Python). If it is missing, Matplotlib falls back to another font and prints warnings; hp.set_graph_theme(rebuild_font_cache=True) refreshes the font cache after installing it.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
import helpers_ps as hp

The components are then available as attributes:

hp.GraphMtplt        # charts
hp.set_graph_theme   # global chart theme
hp.Calcs             # financial calculations
hp.DfStyling         # table images
hp.Ppt               # PowerPoint
hp.Excel             # Excel
hp.PALETA_COLORES    # institutional color palette

Importing the package imports xlwings

import helpers_ps loads all components, including Excel, which imports xlwings. If you see ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'xlwings', install it with pip install xlwings.

docs.title: Set the chart theme (once per session)
docs.text:
hp.set_graph_theme()

It sets the font, the base sizes and the locale used for number formatting in every chart. See GraphMtplt: Theme for the options.

docs.title: Working with the documentation locally
docs.text:
The documentation is built with MkDocs (Material theme). From the root of the repository:

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve          # http://127.0.0.1:8000, reloads on every change
mkdocs build --clean  # generates the static site in ./site

The site is published automatically by the Deploy Docs GitHub Action when the main branch is updated.

docs.title: Benchmark-relative metrics
docs.text:
These functions compare every column against one benchmark column of the same DataFrame. The benchmark is selected by name with benchmark="SPX"; its own result is trivial (beta 1, tracking error 0...).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

Portfolio vs benchmark

To measure a portfolio against its benchmark, put both NAV series in the same DataFrame: df = pd.concat([nav_portfolio.rename("Portfolio"), index_level.rename("Benchmark")], axis=1) and call hp.Calcs.tracking_error(df, benchmark="Benchmark").

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text:
Function Returns What it measures active_return(df, benchmark) DataFrame Per-period return of each asset minus the benchmark. beta(df, benchmark, window=None) Series (or DataFrame if window) Sensitivity to the benchmark: cov(asset, bench) / var(bench). tracking_error(df, benchmark) Series Standard deviation of the active return (annualized by default). rolling_tracking_error(df, benchmark, window=252) DataFrame Tracking error through time. information_ratio(df, benchmark) Series Mean active return / tracking error. rolling_information_ratio(df, benchmark, window=252) DataFrame Information ratio through time. upside_capture(df, benchmark) Series How much of the benchmark's up periods the asset captured. downside_capture(df, benchmark) Series How much of the benchmark's down periods the asset suffered. capture_ratio(df, benchmark) Series upside_capture / downside_capture (> 1 is good). hit_ratio(df, benchmark) Series Share of periods with positive active return. excess_return(df, benchmark, period="qtd") DataFrame Period-to-date return of the asset minus the benchmark, through time. consistency(df, benchmark, period="qtd") Series Share of dates with positive excess return (based on excess_return).

Shared arguments: method ("simple" / "log"), annualize, periods_per_year (252), ddof (1), window, min_periods (see conventions).

bench = "SPX"
table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Beta": hp.Calcs.beta(prices, bench),
    "Tracking error": hp.Calcs.tracking_error(prices, bench),
    "Information ratio": hp.Calcs.information_ratio(prices, bench),
    "Upside capture": hp.Calcs.upside_capture(prices, bench),
    "Downside capture": hp.Calcs.downside_capture(prices, bench),
    "Capture ratio": hp.Calcs.capture_ratio(prices, bench),
    "Hit ratio": hp.Calcs.hit_ratio(prices, bench),
})
table.drop(index=bench).round(3)
Output

      Beta  Tracking error  Information ratio  Upside capture  Downside capture  Capture ratio  Hit ratio
NDX  0.107           0.243             -0.242           0.049             0.257          0.193      0.505
AGG -0.003           0.163             -0.484           0.005            -0.003         -1.576      0.487

Benchmark row

The benchmark compared with itself gives beta=1, tracking_error=0 and information_ratio=NaN (division by zero); drop its row as above when presenting results.

docs.title: Beta
docs.text:
beta(df, benchmark, window=None, method="simple", min_periods=None, ddof=1)

  • window=None: one historical beta per asset (Series).
  • window=N: rolling beta (DataFrame with the same dates), using N observations.

rolling_beta = hp.Calcs.beta(prices, "SPX", window=126).drop(columns="SPX")

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(rolling_beta)
    .graph_line(x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 3})
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".2f")
    .horizontal_lines([0], color="black")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("6-month rolling beta vs S&P 500")
)

docs.title: Tracking error and information ratio
docs.text:
rolling_te = hp.Calcs.rolling_tracking_error(prices, "SPX", window=126)
rolling_ir = hp.Calcs.rolling_information_ratio(prices, "SPX", window=126)

pd.concat({"TE": rolling_te["NDX"], "IR": rolling_ir["NDX"]}, axis=1).dropna().tail(3).round(3)
Output

               TE     IR
2024-12-25  0.258  0.247
2024-12-26  0.258  0.212
2024-12-27  0.256  0.404

Both use the active return asset - benchmark per period. annualize=True multiplies the tracking error by sqrt(periods_per_year).

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(rolling_te[["NDX", "AGG"]].dropna())
    .graph_line(
        series=[{"ticker": "NDX", "color": "#12275A"}, {"ticker": "AGG", "color": "#B7331F"}],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 3},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("Rolling tracking error vs S&P 500")
)

docs.title: Capture ratios and hit ratio
docs.text:
• upside_capture and downside_capture compound the asset's and the benchmark's returns only over the periods in which the benchmark was up / down and divide them. In upside, above 1.0 (100%) is good; in downside, below 1.0 is good.
  • capture_ratio = upside_capture / downside_capture.
  • hit_ratio is the percentage of periods in which the asset beat the benchmark.

Data frequency

These statistics are calculated on the periodicity of your DataFrame. For monthly capture ratios use month-end prices: prices.resample("ME").last().

docs.title: Excess return and consistency (period-to-date)
docs.text:
excess_return(df, benchmark, period="qtd", fallback=True, week_freq="W-FRI") returns the period-to-date return of each asset minus that of the benchmark on every date. period is one of "wtd", "mtd", "qtd", "ytd".

consistency() is the share of dates in which that excess return was positive.

ex_ytd = hp.Calcs.excess_return(prices, "SPX", period="ytd")
cons = hp.Calcs.consistency(prices, "SPX", period="mtd")

pd.DataFrame({"Excess YTD (last)": ex_ytd.iloc[-1], "MTD consistency": cons}).drop(index="SPX").round(3)
Output

     Excess YTD (last)  MTD consistency
NDX             -0.200            0.446
AGG             -0.155            0.444

docs.title: Calcs: Getting Started
docs.text:
Calcs is a collection of financial calculations over a DataFrame of prices: period-to-date returns, performance and risk statistics, drawdowns, benchmark-relative metrics (beta, tracking error, information ratio, capture), Value at Risk, technical indicators and a few helpers to build ranges and relative series.

import helpers_ps as hp

hp.Calcs.total_return(prices)
hp.Calcs.max_drawdown(prices)
hp.Calcs.beta(prices, benchmark="SPX")

Every function is a plain function: DataFrame in, Series / DataFrame out. Results are designed to be plotted straight away with GraphMtplt or shown in a TableSheet.

docs.title: The input: a DataFrame of prices
docs.text:
All functions expect the same layout:

Requirement Detail Index pandas.DatetimeIndex, with no duplicated dates. Unsorted indexes are sorted internally. Columns One column per asset / series, numeric. The column names become the labels of the results. Values Prices or index levels (not returns). Returns are computed internally. Benchmark For benchmark-relative functions, the benchmark is one more column of the same DataFrame, referenced by benchmark="NAME". 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)


prices.tail(3).round(2)
Output

               SPX     NDX     AGG
2024-12-25  120.57  102.20  104.37
2024-12-26  119.14  101.43  104.09
2024-12-27  120.02  102.57  104.05

If the validation fails you get an explicit error:

Error Cause TypeError: The DataFrame index must be a pandas DatetimeIndex. The index is not dates. Use df.set_index("date") after pd.to_datetime. TypeError: The DataFrame contains non-numeric columns: [...] Drop or convert text columns first. ValueError: The DataFrame index contains duplicated values. Remove duplicated dates. ValueError: The DataFrame cannot be empty. Empty DataFrame. ValueError: Benchmark 'X' was not found in the DataFrame. benchmark is not a column.

docs.title: Common conventions
docs.text:
Argument Where Meaning method most functions "simple" (default, percentage returns) or "log" (logarithmic returns). periods_per_year annualized metrics Number of observations per year: 252 daily (default), 52 weekly, 12 monthly. Change it if your data is not daily. annualize volatility, Sharpe, tracking error, IR... True by default. False gives the per-period value. ddof volatility, tracking error... Degrees of freedom of the standard deviation (1 = sample). window rolling versions Number of observations of the rolling window (252 ~ 1 year of daily data). min_periods rolling versions Minimum observations to produce a value (default: the window). prefix technical indicators Template for the output column names ("RSI{w}_" -> RSI14_SPX).

Output type. Functions that summarize the whole history return a pandas.Series indexed by asset (named after the metric, e.g. "Volatility"). Functions that produce a time series return a DataFrame with the same dates.

docs.title: Function index
docs.text:
Group Functions Page Period-to-date wtd, mtd, qtd, ytd Returns and performance Performance total_return, annualized_return, volatility, sharpe_ratio, downside_std, sortino_ratio Returns and performance Drawdown drawdown, max_drawdown, calmar_ratio Returns and performance Benchmark-relative active_return, beta, tracking_error, rolling_tracking_error, information_ratio, rolling_information_ratio, upside_capture, downside_capture, capture_ratio, hit_ratio, excess_return, consistency Benchmark-relative Risk value_at_risk, expected_shortfall Risk Technical indicators rsi, sma, ema, zscore, bollinger_bands, macd, momentum, momentum_sma Technical indicators Ranges and transformations mean_std_bands, relative, rank_percentile Transformations Object-oriented wrapper Metrics Metrics class

The full signatures are in the API reference.

docs.title: A first analysis
docs.text:
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Total return": hp.Calcs.total_return(prices),
    "Ann. return": hp.Calcs.annualized_return(prices),
    "Volatility": hp.Calcs.volatility(prices),
    "Sharpe (rf 3%)": hp.Calcs.sharpe_ratio(prices, risk_free_rate=0.03),
    "Max drawdown": hp.Calcs.max_drawdown(prices),
})
summary.round(3)
Output

     Total return  Ann. return  Volatility  Sharpe (rf 3%)  Max drawdown
SPX         0.196        0.091       0.150           0.455        -0.122
NDX         0.039        0.019       0.204           0.046        -0.178
AGG         0.037        0.018       0.062          -0.168        -0.087

Because every metric is a Series indexed by asset, they combine naturally into one table with pd.DataFrame({...}), which you can then format and export with DfStyling.

docs.title: The Metrics class
docs.text:
Metrics is an object-oriented wrapper over a price DataFrame. You create it once and call methods that mirror many of the functions of the module, without passing the DataFrame every time. It adds one feature the functions do not have: naming columns through a description table.

Which one should I use?

For new code prefer the functions (hp.Calcs.volatility(df)): they cover more metrics (wtd, rolling versions, sharpe_ratio, macd...), validate the input and have complete docstrings. Use Metrics if you already have code built on it or if you need assign_names.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

docs.title: Creating the object
docs.text:
hp.Calcs.Metrics(data_frame, descripcion=None, fallback=True)

Argument Description data_frame Prices: DatetimeIndex and one column per asset. Not empty (ValueError), with a date index (TypeError). descripcion Optional. DataFrame indexed by ticker with a column Nombre (display name). fallback Same meaning as in the functions: for ytd / mtd / qtd, if there is no previous period-end, use the first price of the period. 

m = hp.Calcs.Metrics(data_frame=prices)
m.ytd().tail(1).round(4)
Output

               SPX     NDX     AGG
2024-12-27  0.1735 -0.0266  0.0181

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Equivalent function Notes ytd(), mtd(), qtd() ytd, mtd, qtd drawdown(method="simple", min_price=1e-6) drawdown std_downside(method, target_return, annualize, periods_per_year) downside_std beta(benchmark, window=None, method="simple") beta upside_capture(benchmark), downside_capture(benchmark), capture_ratio(benchmark) same names tracking_error(benchmark, ...), information_ratio(benchmark, ...) same names var(confidence, method, returns_method, horizon) value_at_risk excess_return(benchmark, period="qtd"), consistency(benchmark, period="qtd") same names rsi(window, prefix), sma(windows, ...), ema(windows, ...) same names ranges(desviaciones, prefix) mean_std_bands Default column prefix Media({w}sigma)_. relative(...), momentum(...), momentum_sma(...), rank_percentile() assign_names(data_frame=None) not available as a function Renames columns using descripcion. 

pd.DataFrame({
    "Beta": m.beta("SPX"),
    "Tracking error": m.tracking_error("SPX"),
    "VaR 95%": m.var(),
}).round(4)
Output

       Beta  Tracking error  VaR 95%
SPX  1.0000          0.0000   0.0147
NDX  0.1075          0.2435   0.0220
AGG -0.0025          0.1626   0.0064

docs.title: Using descriptions to rename columns
docs.text:
When descripcion is given, the class builds a relation table that maps each column to a readable name. Columns of the form "PREFIX-TICKER" are matched using the part after the dash. assign_names() then renames the columns of any result that contains the tickers in their names.

description = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Nombre": ["S&P 500", "Nasdaq 100", "Global Aggregate"]},
    index=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

m = hp.Calcs.Metrics(data_frame=prices, descripcion=description)
m.assign_names(m.rsi().tail(1))
Output

            RSI14_S&P 500  RSI14_Nasdaq 100  RSI14_Global Aggregate
2024-12-27      40.475202         35.055255               44.683135

In-place renaming

assign_names() modifies the columns of the DataFrame you pass and returns it. When called without arguments it renames m.data_frame itself, so make a copy first if you still need the original tickers.

API reference of the calculations

docs.title: Returns, performance and drawdowns
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

docs.title: Period-to-date returns
docs.text:
wtd, mtd, qtd and ytd return a DataFrame with the same shape as the input. On each date they give the return since the end of the previous week / month / quarter / year, so the last row is the current "to-date" figure and the whole series can be charted.

Function Base price Arguments wtd(df, fallback=True, week_freq="W-FRI") Last price of the previous week (weeks end on Friday by default) week_freq: pandas weekly frequency mtd(df, fallback=True) Last price of the previous month qtd(df, fallback=True) Last price of the previous quarter ytd(df, fallback=True) Last price of the previous year

fallback=True uses the first price of the current period as base when the series starts in the middle of a period (no previous period-end exists), so the first periods are not lost as NaN.

last = pd.DataFrame({
    "WTD": hp.Calcs.wtd(prices).iloc[-1],
    "MTD": hp.Calcs.mtd(prices).iloc[-1],
    "QTD": hp.Calcs.qtd(prices).iloc[-1],
    "YTD": hp.Calcs.ytd(prices).iloc[-1],
})
last.round(4)
Output

        WTD     MTD     QTD     YTD
SPX -0.0071 -0.0266  0.0607  0.1735
NDX -0.0200 -0.0911 -0.0340 -0.0266
AGG -0.0134  0.0123 -0.0030  0.0181


g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(hp.Calcs.ytd(prices))
    .graph_line(
        series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}, {"ticker": "NDX"}, {"ticker": "AGG"}],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 3},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides()
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("Year-to-date return")
)

Calendar-day data

Period-to-date calculations assume prices may be stored per calendar day with non-trading days forward-filled (for example a Bloomberg PX_LAST download). They work equally with business-day data.

docs.title: Performance statistics
docs.text:
Function Returns Key arguments total_return(df, method="simple") Series: cumulative return over the whole sample method annualized_return(df, periods_per_year=252, method="simple") Series: compound annual growth rate periods_per_year, method volatility(df, method="simple", annualize=True, periods_per_year=252, ddof=1) Series: standard deviation of returns annualize, periods_per_year, ddof sharpe_ratio(df, risk_free_rate=0.0, ...) Series: excess return / volatility risk_free_rate (annual, e.g. 0.03) downside_std(df, target_return=0.0, annualize=False, ...) DataFrame with one column std_downside target_return (per period), annualize sortino_ratio(df, target_return=0.0, ...) Series: excess return / downside deviation target_return (annual) 

stats = pd.DataFrame({
    "Total return": hp.Calcs.total_return(prices),
    "Annualized return": hp.Calcs.annualized_return(prices),
    "Volatility": hp.Calcs.volatility(prices),
    "Sharpe (rf=3%)": hp.Calcs.sharpe_ratio(prices, risk_free_rate=0.03),
    "Sortino": hp.Calcs.sortino_ratio(prices),
})
stats.round(3)
Output

     Total return  Annualized return  Volatility  Sharpe (rf=3%)  Sortino
SPX         0.196              0.091       0.150           0.455    0.959
NDX         0.039              0.019       0.204           0.046    0.276
AGG         0.037              0.018       0.062          -0.168    0.448

docs.title: Not daily data?
docs.text:
Tell the function how many observations a year has. With monthly prices:

monthly_prices = prices.resample("ME").last()

hp.Calcs.volatility(monthly_prices, periods_per_year=12)
hp.Calcs.annualized_return(monthly_prices, periods_per_year=12)
hp.Calcs.sharpe_ratio(monthly_prices, risk_free_rate=0.03, periods_per_year=12)

docs.title: Rolling volatility
docs.text:
The functions summarize the whole sample. For a rolling statistic compute returns and use pandas:

daily = prices.pct_change().dropna()
rolling_vol = daily.rolling(63).std() * np.sqrt(252)          # 3-month rolling, annualized

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(rolling_vol)
    .graph_line(x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 3})
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("3-month rolling volatility")
)

rolling_tracking_error() and rolling_information_ratio() (see Benchmark-relative) do this for you against a benchmark.

docs.title: Drawdowns
docs.text:
Function Returns drawdown(df, method="simple", min_price=1e-6) DataFrame: distance (<= 0) from the running maximum on every date max_drawdown(df, method="simple", min_price=1e-6) Series: the worst drawdown of each asset calmar_ratio(df, periods_per_year=252) Series: annualized return / absolute max drawdown 

pd.DataFrame({
    "Max drawdown": hp.Calcs.max_drawdown(prices),
    "Calmar": hp.Calcs.calmar_ratio(prices),
}).round(3)
Output

     Max drawdown  Calmar
SPX        -0.122   0.743
NDX        -0.178   0.105
AGG        -0.087   0.205


g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(hp.Calcs.drawdown(prices))

docs.title: value_at_risk
docs.text:
value_at_risk(df, confidence=0.95, method="historical", returns_method="simple", horizon=1)

method How it is computed "historical" Empirical quantile of the observed returns (no distribution assumed). "gaussian" Normal distribution with the sample mean and standard deviation. "cornish_fisher" Gaussian VaR adjusted by the skewness and kurtosis of the sample. 

pd.DataFrame({
    "Historical 95%": hp.Calcs.value_at_risk(prices),
    "Gaussian 95%": hp.Calcs.value_at_risk(prices, method="gaussian"),
    "Cornish-Fisher 95%": hp.Calcs.value_at_risk(prices, method="cornish_fisher"),
    "Historical 99%": hp.Calcs.value_at_risk(prices, confidence=0.99),
    "Gaussian 99%, 10 days": hp.Calcs.value_at_risk(prices, confidence=0.99, method="gaussian", horizon=10),
}).round(4)
Output

     Historical 95%  Gaussian 95%  Cornish-Fisher 95%  Historical 99%  Gaussian 99%, 10 days
SPX          0.0147        0.0152              0.0152          0.0218                 0.0656
NDX          0.0220        0.0210              0.0210          0.0291                 0.0930
AGG          0.0064        0.0063              0.0064          0.0087                 0.0278
  • confidence must be between 0 and 1 (ValueError otherwise).
  • horizon is a number of observations of your DataFrame (10 for ten trading days of daily data). The "historical" method uses rolling compounded returns over the horizon; the parametric methods scale the mean by horizon and the volatility by sqrt(horizon).

docs.text:
expected_shortfall(df, confidence=0.95, returns_method="simple", horizon=1)

Also called Conditional VaR: the average loss in the cases that exceed the VaR. It is always larger than or equal to the VaR of the same confidence.

pd.DataFrame({
    "VaR 95%": hp.Calcs.value_at_risk(prices),
    "ES 95%": hp.Calcs.expected_shortfall(prices),

SPX   0.0147  0.0197
NDX   0.0220  0.0271
AGG   0.0064  0.0077

docs.text:
Indicator functions take the price DataFrame and return a DataFrame with the same dates. The output column names combine a prefix and the asset name (SMA50_SPX), so several assets and several windows can live in the same result. Change the prefix with prefix="..." (use {w} as the placeholder for the window).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)
Function Output columns Arguments (default) sma(df, windows=None, min_periods=None, prefix="SMA{w}_") SMA50_SPX... windows ([50]) ema(df, windows=None, min_periods=None, prefix="EMA{w}_") EMA27_SPX... windows ([27]) rsi(df, window=14, prefix="RSI{w}_") RSI14_SPX... (0-100) window zscore(df, window=252, min_periods=None, prefix="ZScore{w}_") ZScore252_SPX... rolling z-score of the price bollinger_bands(df, window=20, num_std=2.0, min_periods=None) BB_Middle20_, BB_Upper20_, BB_Lower20_ + asset macd(df, fast=12, slow=26, signal=9) MACD_, MACDSignal_, MACDHist_ + asset momentum(df, windows=None, prefix="MomentumSimple{w}_") MomentumSimple15_SPX... z-score of the rolling compounded return of each window; windows ([15, 30]) momentum_sma(df, prefix="MomentumSMA_") MomentumSMA_SPX... discrete score 1 to 5 (1 = bearish, 3 = neutral, 5 = bullish) from the 5- and 15-day moving averages

docs.title: Z-score, momentum
docs.text:
• zscore: (price - rolling mean) / rolling std over window observations. Useful to flag stretched prices (|z| > 2).
  • momentum: for each window, the rolling compounded return is standardized with its own rolling mean and standard deviation (a z-score of the return).
  • momentum_sma: classifies each date with a score from 1 to 5 by comparing the price with the 15-day moving average, the slope of that average and the gap between the 5- and 15-day averages. It uses fixed windows (5 and 15) and has no window argument.

hp.Calcs.zscore(prices, window=126).dropna().tail(2).round(2)
Output

2024-12-26           0.11          -0.78           0.51
2024-12-27           0.35          -0.55           0.45

mean_std_bands(df, std_multipliers=None, prefix="Mean({w}std)_")

Static reference levels mean + k x std of the whole sample, repeated on every date so they can be drawn as horizontal lines (valuation bands, mean reversion). The default multipliers are [-1, 0, 1].     {"ticker": "SPX", "relative": "AGG", "operation": "-", "name": "SPX - AGG"},

])

docs.title: rank_percentile
docs.text:
rank_percentile(df, value=None) returns, per column, the percentile (0-1) of a value within the historical distribution of that column.

value What is ranked None The last row of df. number That number. Requires df with exactly one column. one-row DataFrame One value per column (same columns as df). 

last_rank = hp.Calcs.rank_percentile(prices)                  # where is today vs history?
what_if = hp.Calcs.rank_percentile(prices, value=pd.DataFrame([[110, 100, 104]], columns=prices.columns))

pd.DataFrame({"Today": last_rank, "If SPX=110, NDX=100, AGG=104": what_if}).round(3)
Output

     Today  If SPX=110, NDX=100, AGG=104
SPX  0.850                         0.601
NDX  0.621                         0.438
AGG  0.815                         0.806

A percentile of 0.85 means today's value is higher than 85% of the history. It combines well with the distribution chart: its {percentile} tag field shows the same idea directly on the histogram.

docs.title: Functional styling (without a sheet)
docs.text:
Every styling operation of TableSheet also exists as a function that takes a DataFrame or a Styler and returns a Styler. Use them when you want the styled table itself: to show it in a notebook, export it to Excel, or build your own Styler pipeline.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

simple = pd.DataFrame(
    {"YTD": [0.121, 0.084, 0.032, 0.067], "1Y": [0.156, 0.101, 0.041, 0.083], "3Y": [0.092, 0.075, 0.028, 0.061]},
    index=["Equity", "Bonds", "Cash", "Total"],
)

All functions are available as hp.DfStyling.<name>:

Function Description style_table(obj, font_family, font_size, text_color, background_color, text_align, header_styles, index_styles, data_styles, column_header_styles, row_index_styles, show_index_names, corner_styles) General look (same arguments as the method of TableSheet). style_cell(obj, row, column, styles) CSS on one cell. style_cells(obj, rows, columns, styles) CSS on rows x columns. border_cell(obj, row, column, position, width, color, line_style) Border on one side of a cell. border_cells(obj, rows, columns, position, width, color, line_style) Border on one side of many cells. highlight_rows(obj, rows, styles, include_index, index_level) Highlight rows (default: bold and boxed). highlight_columns(obj, columns, styles, include_header, header_level) Highlight columns. border_rows(obj, rows, position, styles) Horizontal line across complete rows. border_columns(obj, columns, position, include_header, header_level, styles) Vertical line next to columns. text_color_by_range(value, ranges) / background_color_by_range(value, ranges) Return the CSS ("color: ...") for one value; use with Styler.map.

obj is a DataFrame or an existing Styler; the result is always a Styler, so calls chain through the variable:

styled = hp.DfStyling.style_table(
    simple,
    font_size=11,
    text_align="center",
    header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"},
)
styled = hp.DfStyling.highlight_rows(styled, "Total", styles={"background-color": "#FFF2CC"})
styled = hp.DfStyling.border_rows(styled, "Cash", styles={"width": "2px", "color": "#12275A"})
styled = styled.format("{:.1%}")

type(styled).__name__
Output

'Styler'

docs.title: Conditional color of a single value
docs.text:
text_color_by_range(value, ranges) and background_color_by_range(value, ranges) are the per-value helpers behind the sheet methods. They return a CSS declaration and are meant for Styler.map:

import numpy as np

ranges = {(-np.inf, 0): "#B7331F", (0, 0.05): "#C9A227", (0.05, np.inf): "#1E8449"}

print(hp.DfStyling.text_color_by_range(0.08, ranges))
print(hp.DfStyling.background_color_by_range(0.08, {(0.05, np.inf): "#D9EAD3"}))

colored = simple.style.map(lambda v: hp.DfStyling.text_color_by_range(v, ranges))
Output

color: #1E8449
background-color: #D9EAD3

Intervals are lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive; a missing value or a value outside every interval returns an empty string.

docs.title: Export a styled table to Excel
docs.text:
A Styler keeps fonts, colors and borders when written to Excel with to_excel_closed_styled:

hp.Excel.to_excel_closed_styled(styled, "report.xlsx", sheet_name="Performance")

Only the styles that Excel understands are preserved (colors, bold / italic, borders, alignment, number formats set with format).

API reference of DfStyling

docs.title: DfStyling: Getting Started
docs.text:
DfStyling turns pandas DataFrames into presentation-ready images. The central class is TableSheet: it holds one or several tables (and charts), records the styling you apply to each, and composes everything (sheet title, panel titles, notes, sources) into one image that you can preview in a notebook, save as PNG / PDF / SVG, or insert into a presentation.

import helpers_ps as hp

sheet = (
    hp.DfStyling.TableSheet(df, width_in=7)
    .style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center")
    .format("{:.1f}")
    .panel(title="Yield changes", subtitle="Basis points")
    .add_source("Source: Bloomberg")
)
sheet.preview()                      # show it in a notebook
sheet.save("yield_changes.png")      # write it to disk

Like GraphMtplt, every method returns the sheet, so everything chains.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Tables are drawn by a headless Chromium browser (through Playwright), so the HTML/CSS of a pandas Styler is reproduced exactly.

Need How playwright pip install playwright A Chromium-based browser Any Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge installed on the machine is used automatically. Otherwise run python -m playwright install chromium. The font Inter is the default font of titles and notes. If it is not installed, DejaVu Sans is used.

You can point to a specific browser with a custom renderer:

from helpers_ps.DfStyling import PlaywrightRenderer

renderer = PlaywrightRenderer(chrome_path=r"C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe")
sheet = hp.DfStyling.TableSheet(df, renderer=renderer)

Browser launch

The browser is launched once per render, with all tables of the sheet rendered in the same batch, and results are cached by content. Changing a title, the layout or the spacing never launches the browser again; changing the styling of one table only re-renders that table.

docs.title: Your first table
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

yields = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "1M": [5.0, -9.0, 3.2],
        "3M": [8.0, 39.0, -1.5],
        "1Y": [12.0, 25.0, 4.0],
        "5Y": [-3.0, -11.0, 7.5],
    },
    index=["UST 2Y", "UST 10Y", "Bund 10Y"],
)


sheet = (
    hp.DfStyling.TableSheet(yields, width_in=6)
    .style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center")
    .format("{:+.1f}")
    .panel(title="Change in yields", subtitle="Basis points")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

In a notebook, sheet.preview() shows the result. sheet.save("table.png") writes it.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
Concept What it is Sheet The whole image: optional title, a grid of panels, general notes and sources. Panel One element of the grid: a table (a DataFrame / Styler plus its styling) or an image (usually a chart). Active panel(s) The styling methods apply to the active panels. The newest panel is active; select others with on("name") or on() for all. Recipe A table is stored as its source plus the ordered list of operations applied to it. The Styler is rebuilt from that recipe whenever needed, so re-running a notebook cell never accumulates CSS.

Typical flow:

  1. Create the sheet with one or several DataFrames (TableSheet(df), TableSheet({"a": df1, "b": df2}), or add_table()).
  2. Style each table (style_table, format, borders, highlights, color ranges...). See Styling tables.
  3. Describe each panel (panel(title=..., notes=...)) and the sheet (add_title, add_note, add_source).
  4. Arrange the panels on a grid (layout) and set the size (Panels, charts and layout, Sheet appearance and output).
  5. Output: preview(), save(), to_bytes(), figure.

docs.title: Method overview
docs.text:
Group Methods Page Create / select panels TableSheet(...), add_table, add_image, on, remove, panel_names Panels Panel texts panel(title, subtitle, notes, align, valign, scale, ...) The complete signatures are in the API reference.

TableSheet uses them under the hood. They are useful when you want the styled DataFrame itself, for example to export it to Excel with to_excel_closed_styled. See Functional styling.

docs.title: Sheet appearance and output
docs.text:
This page covers the sheet-level settings (size, margins, text styles, rules, scaling) and how to preview, save and reuse the final image.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

TableSheet = hp.DfStyling.TableSheet

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"1M": [5, -9, 3], "3M": [8, 39, -2], "1Y": [12, 25, 4]},
    index=["UST 2Y", "UST 10Y", "Bund 10Y"],
)

docs.title: Sheet texts
docs.text:
Method Description add_title(text, *, size=None, color=None, weight=None) Sheet title above all panels. "" removes it. add_note(*notes, size=None, color=None) Appends general notes below the panels (above the sources). size / color apply to all notes, including those of each panel. add_source(*sources, size=None, color=None) Replaces the source lines at the bottom. Called with no arguments it clears them.

Sources and copyright

Source lines are printed exactly as written; nothing (prefix, license, copyright) is added automatically. Write "Source: Bloomberg" or "© My Company" yourself.

sheet = (
    TableSheet(df, width_in=6)
    .style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center")
    .panel(title="Change in yields", subtitle="Basis points", notes="MTD: month to date.")
    .add_title("Rates monitor")
    .add_note("Changes are measured against the previous close.", size=7)
    .add_source("Source: Bloomberg", "Prepared by Portfolio Solutions", size=6.5)
)

docs.title: config_layout: every visual parameter
docs.text:
config_layout(**changes) changes any field of SheetStyle, validating it before applying (nothing changes if a value is invalid). The same names can be given to the TableSheet(...) constructor. Fields that accept None return to automatic when set to None.

sheet.config_layout(width_in=13.33, height_in=7.5, scale="fit")
sheet.config_layout(wspace=None)        # back to col_gap_in

docs.title: SheetStyle fields
docs.text:
Size

Field Default Description width_in 8.0 Image width in inches. height_in None Image height in inches. None = computed from the content. When set, the image has exactly that height: sources are anchored to the bottom, panels that do not fit are scaled down and free space follows valign. valign "top" Where the panels sit when height_in leaves free space: "top", "center", "bottom". dpi 200 Resolution of rendered tables and of the exported image. font_family "Inter" Font of titles, notes and sources. A comma-separated list is accepted; falls back to DejaVu Sans.

Spacing (subplots_adjust semantics, None = automatic)

Field Default Description left, right None Grid edges as a fraction of the image width. None uses margin_in. bottom, top None Grid edges as a fraction of the height measured from the bottom. Require height_in. wspace, hspace None Space between columns / rows as a fraction of the average column width / row height. None uses col_gap_in / row_gap_in. margin_in 0.45 Side margin in inches. col_gap_in, row_gap_in 0.30 Gaps in inches. pad_top_in, pad_bottom_in 0.15, 0.20 Space above the top rule and below the last source line.

Text

Field Default Description header_size, header_color, header_weight 18, #111111, bold Sheet title. title_size, title_color, title_weight 12, #111111, bold Default panel titles. subtitle_size, subtitle_color 9, #666666 Panel subtitles. title_gap_in 0.08 Gap between a panel title block and its table. footer_size, footer_color 9, #666666 Default size / color of notes and sources. note_size, note_color None Notes (panel and general). None uses footer_*. source_size, source_color None Source lines. None uses footer_*. line_spacing 1.5 Line height as a multiple of the font size. wrap_text True Wrap titles and notes to the width of their cell.

Rules and canvas

Field Default Description line_color, line_width #D9D9D9, 1.2 Color and thickness (points) of the two horizontal rules. top_line, bottom_line True Show the rule above the content / above the sources. background "white" Canvas color. scale "uniform" How panels are resized (below). resampling "lanczos" Filter used to resize table images ("lanczos", "bicubic", "bilinear", "nearest"). table_font_px 14 Base font size of rendered tables in CSS pixels (overridden by style_table(font_size=...)). zebra True Alternate row shading.

You can also build the style once and reuse it across sheets:

from helpers_ps.DfStyling import SheetStyle

house_style = SheetStyle(width_in=13.33, height_in=7.5, header_size=20, line_color="#12275A")
sheet = TableSheet(df, style=house_style)

docs.title: Scale: how panels are resized
docs.text:
scale Behavior "uniform" (default) The same scale for every table, the largest that fits all cells. Tables of the same sheet show the same visual font size. "fit" Stretches each panel to the width of its cell. "natural" Keeps the real size (pixels / dpi inches) and only shrinks panels that do not fit.

Each panel can override the sheet value with panel(scale=...). Image panels treat "uniform" as "natural".

docs.title: Spacing
docs.text:
subplots_adjust(left=None, bottom=None, right=None, top=None, wspace=None, hspace=None) positions the grid like matplotlib.pyplot.subplots_adjust. Only the values you pass change; every value is a fraction:

  • left, right: edges as a fraction of the image width.
  • bottom, top: edges as a fraction of the height measured from the bottom (top=0.9 leaves 10% above). They require height_in.
  • wspace, hspace: space between columns / rows relative to the average column width / row height.

The sheet title and the sources are aligned with the left edge of the grid.

docs.title: A slide-sized image
docs.text:
For a 16:9 slide use width_in=13.33, height_in=7.5:

sheet = (
    TableSheet({"a": df, "b": df * 2}, width_in=13.33, height_in=7.5)
    .on().style_table(font_size=14, text_align="center",
                      header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"},
                      corner_styles={"background-color": "#12275A"})
    .on("a").panel(title="Today")
    .on("b").panel(title="Scenario")
    .layout(nrows=1)
    .subplots_adjust(left=0.06, right=0.94, top=0.80, bottom=0.14, wspace=0.12)
    .add_title("Rates monitor")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)


sheet.size_in
Output

(13.33, 7.5)

docs.title: Output methods
docs.text:
Method / property Returns Description preview() the sheet Shows the sheet in a Jupyter notebook (no file). render() the sheet Pre-renders the tables so later outputs are immediate. Optional: every output renders on demand. save(path=None, *, dir=None, name=None, fmt=None, transparent=False) the sheet Writes a file. Give either path, or name (with an optional dir). The format comes from fmt or the file extension (png if none): "png", "pdf", "svg", "jpg". The dir folder is created if missing. last_path (property) Path or None Path written by the last save. to_bytes(fmt="png", *, transparent=False) bytes Encoded image. to_array() ndarray (H, W, 3) RGB pixels of the final image. figure (property) matplotlib.figure.Figure The composed sheet, rebuilt on every access from the cached table images. size_in (property) (width, height) Final size in inches. 

import os

sheet.save(dir="out", name="rates_monitor", fmt="png")
sheet.save("out/rates_monitor.pdf")
print(sheet.last_path)
sorted(os.listdir("out"))
Output

out/rates_monitor.pdf
['rates_monitor.pdf', 'rates_monitor.png']

save has the same naming as GraphMtplt

sheet.save(dir="out", name="lamina") mirrors graph.save(dir=..., name=...). Note, though, that TableSheet.save writes a file and returns the sheet, while GraphMtplt.save returns a buffer.

docs.title: Insert in PowerPoint
docs.text:
to_bytes() can be inserted directly in a slide with python-pptx:

import io
from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches

prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width, prs.slide_height = Inches(13.33), Inches(7.5)
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])        # blank layout

slide.shapes.add_picture(io.BytesIO(sheet.to_bytes()), 0, 0, width=prs.slide_width)
prs.save("monitor.pptx")
os.path.exists("monitor.pptx")
Output

True

docs.title: Cache and renderer
docs.text:
Object Description RenderCache(max_mb=256) LRU cache of rendered table images, keyed by content (the HTML that is rendered). Pass cache=RenderCache(max_mb=0) to TableSheet to disable caching. Attributes: hits, misses, size_mb; methods: get, put, clear. clear_render_cache() Empties the process-wide cache shared by all sheets. PlaywrightRenderer(chrome_path=None, channels=("chrome", "msedge", "chromium", None), timeout_ms=30000, launch_args=()) Renders HTML to images with headless Chromium. Customize it to choose the browser executable or pass launch arguments.

You can supply your own renderer as any callable renderer(documents, dpi) -> list of RGB uint8 arrays.

Jupyter on Windows

Jupyter installs an event-loop policy that cannot spawn subprocesses. PlaywrightRenderer runs the browser in a dedicated thread with the right policy, so it works inside notebooks without extra steps. If no browser can be launched, the error lists every attempted channel and how to fix it (python -m playwright install chromium, or install Chrome / Edge).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix No Chromium-based browser could be launched No Chrome / Edge and no Playwright Chromium. python -m playwright install chromium or use PlaywrightRenderer(chrome_path=...). ImportError: Playwright is required to render tables Playwright is not installed. pip install playwright. top/bottom ignored or an error at render time They need a fixed height_in. Set height_in. Title font looks different from Inter Inter is not installed in the system. Install the font or set font_family. Table text too small next to the title scale="uniform" shrinks all tables to fit the narrowest cell. Use scale="fit" on the panel, or increase width_in.

docs.title: Panels, charts and layout
docs.text:
A TableSheet is a grid of panels. A panel is either a table (DataFrame / Styler) or an image (a GraphMtplt chart, a Matplotlib figure, a PIL image, a file...). This page explains how to create panels, give them names and titles, select which ones a styling call affects and arrange them on the grid.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

TableSheet = hp.DfStyling.TableSheet

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

df_yield = pd.DataFrame(
    {"1M": [5, -9, 3], "3M": [8, 39, -2], "1Y": [12, 25, 4]},
    index=["UST 2Y", "UST 10Y", "Bund 10Y"],
)
df_spreads = pd.DataFrame(
    {"1M": [-2.0, 4.5, 1.0], "3M": [3.0, 6.0, -1.5], "1Y": [8.0, 11.0, 2.0]},
    index=["IG", "HY", "EM"],
)

dates = pd.bdate_range("2024-01-02", periods=250)
curve_df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"UST 10Y": 4 + rng.normal(0, 0.04, len(dates)).cumsum()},
    index=dates,
)

docs.title: Creating the sheet
docs.text:
TableSheet(dataframe=None, *, names=None, style=None, renderer=None, cache=None, nrows=None, ncols=None, width_ratios=None, **style_options)

dataframe can be:

Input Result A DataFrame, Styler or Series One table panel. A list of tables Several panels named panel_0, panel_1... (or names=[...]). A dictionary {name: table} Several panels with your names. None An empty sheet; add panels later with add_table / add_image.

Any SheetStyle field (width_in=11, height_in=7.5, font_family=...) can be passed as keyword argument.

TableSheet(df_yield)                                         # one table
TableSheet([df_yield, df_spreads], names=["yield", "spreads"])
TableSheet({"yield": df_yield, "spreads": df_spreads}, width_in=12)

docs.title: Adding panels later
docs.text:
Method Description add_table(dataframe, name=None, *, activate=True) Adds a table panel. A Styler is copied, never modified. add_image(image, name=None, *, activate=True) Adds an image panel (see below). remove(*keys) Removes panels (by name or position) and their cells in an explicit layout; rows / columns left empty are dropped. panel_names (property) List of panel names in creation order.

By default the new panel becomes the only active one, so the styling calls that follow apply to it. Use activate=False to keep the previous selection.

docs.title: Selecting panels
docs.text:
on(*keys) chooses the panels that the next calls apply to. Keys are names or positions (negatives allowed); no arguments selects every panel.

sheet = (
    TableSheet({"yield": df_yield, "spreads": df_spreads}, width_in=9)
    .on().style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center",
                      header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"},
                      corner_styles={"background-color": "#12275A"})
    .on("yield").format("{:+.0f}").panel(title="Change in yields", subtitle="Basis points")
    .on("spreads").format("{:+.1f}").panel(title="Change in spreads", subtitle="Basis points")
    .layout(nrows=1)                       # side by side
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

docs.title: Panel texts and geometry: panel
docs.text:
panel(*, title=None, subtitle=None, notes=None, align=None, valign=None, scale=None, title_size=None, title_color=None, title_weight=None)

None leaves a setting unchanged; use "" (or [] for notes) to clear it. It applies to the active panels.

Argument Description title, subtitle Text above the table (subtitle is smaller and gray). notes A string or list of strings below the panel. Replaces the previous ones. align "left" (default), "center", "right": horizontal position when the panel is narrower than its cell. valign "top", "center", "bottom": vertical position when the cell is taller than the panel (for example a panel that spans several rows). scale Overrides the sheet's scale for this panel. title_size, title_color, title_weight Style overrides of this panel's title. 
sheet.on("yield").panel(
    title="Change in yields",
    subtitle="Basis points",
    notes=["MTD: month to date.", "Source: Bloomberg."],
)

docs.title: Charts as panels: add_image
docs.text:
add_image(image, name=None, *, activate=True) accepts a GraphMtplt object directly, a Matplotlib Figure, a NumPy array, a PIL image, encoded bytes, or a file path. Figures (and objects with a _fig, such as GraphMtplt) are rasterized when the sheet is rendered with the sheet's dpi, so they always reflect their current state.

chart = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(curve_df)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "UST 10Y", "color": "#12275A"}],
                x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 2})
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".2f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
)

sheet = (
    TableSheet(df_yield, names=["yield"], width_in=11)
    .style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center")
    .format("{:+.0f}")
    .panel(title="Change in yields", subtitle="Basis points")
    .add_image(chart, name="curve")
    .panel(title="UST 10Y", scale="fit")
    .layout([["yield", "curve"]], width_ratios=[2, 3])
    .add_title("Rates monitor")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

Chart size

Image panels treat scale="uniform" as "natural": a chart keeps its real size and is only shrunk if it does not fit. Use panel(scale="fit") to make it fill the width of its cell. Choose the chart's size when you create it with GraphMtplt.plot(figsize=(w, h)).

docs.title: Arranging panels: layout
docs.text:
layout(rows=None, *, nrows=None, ncols=None, width_ratios=None)

Form Result layout() Stack the panels vertically (the default). layout(nrows=1) One row: panels side by side. layout(ncols=2) / layout(nrows=2) Fill a grid row by row in creation order. If only one is given, the other is the smallest that fits. layout([["a", "b"], ["c", "c"]]) Explicit grid, like matplotlib.pyplot.subplot_mosaic. Repeating a name makes the panel span several cells. Use None or "." for an empty cell. width_ratios=[1, 2] Relative width of each column (one value per column).

Row heights follow the content of each row.

sheet = (
    TableSheet({"yield": df_yield, "spreads": df_spreads}, width_in=11)
    .on().style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center")
    .on("yield").panel(title="Yields")
    .on("spreads").panel(title="Spreads")
    .add_image(chart, name="curve").panel(title="UST 10Y", scale="fit")
    .layout([["yield", "curve"], ["spreads", "curve"]], width_ratios=[3, 4])   # the chart spans both rows
    .on("curve").panel(valign="center")
)

Rectangles only

A repeated name must occupy a rectangular block of cells (otherwise ValueError). A row with fewer entries is stretched when its length divides the number of columns ([["a", "b"], ["c"]] makes c span both columns).

docs.title: Spacing between panels
docs.text:
Grid spacing follows matplotlib.subplots_adjust semantics (see Sheet appearance and output):

sheet.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.15, hspace=0.25)       # fractions of the average width / height
sheet.config_layout(col_gap_in=0.4, row_gap_in=0.3)    # or fixed gaps in inches

docs.title: Styling tables
docs.text:
Every styling method of TableSheet acts on the active panel(s) (the most recently added one by default; see on()). Calls are recorded in the order you write them and replayed to build the final table, so the latest call wins when two rules set the same CSS property.

All style arguments are plain CSS properties in dictionaries: {"background-color": "#12275A", "color": "white", "font-weight": "bold"}.

The examples use two tables. A simple one and a MultiIndex one with the index levels Metric, Period and Rating.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

TableSheet = hp.DfStyling.TableSheet

simple = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "YTD": [0.121, 0.084, 0.032, 0.067],
        "1Y": [0.156, 0.101, 0.041, 0.083],
        "3Y": [0.092, 0.075, 0.028, 0.061],
    },
    index=["Equity", "Bonds", "Cash", "Total"],
)

index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [["Δ Yield", "Δ Spreads"], ["MTD", "YTD"], ["AAA", "AA+", "A"]],
    names=["Metric", "Period", "Rating"],
)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
multi = pd.DataFrame(
    rng.integers(-30, 40, size=(len(index), 4)),
    index=index,
    columns=["1M", "3M", "1Y", "5Y"],
)

docs.title: style_table: the general look
docs.text:
One call sets typography, colors and the style of headers, index and data cells. Every argument is optional.

Argument Applies to Example font_family, font_size, text_color, background_color, text_align header, index and data cells font_size=11, text_align="center" header_styles all column-header cells {"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"} index_styles all row-index cells (every level) {"background-color": "#F2F2F2", "font-weight": "normal"} data_styles all data cells {"border-bottom": "1px solid #E5E5E5"} column_header_styles selected headers list of {"columns": [...], "styles": {...}, "level": n} row_index_styles selected index labels list of {"values": [...], "level": n or name, "styles": {...}, "parent": (...)} corner_styles the corner above the index and the index-names row {"background-color": "#12275A"} show_index_names the row with the index level names False hides it

font_size is in pixels when numeric (11 = "11px") or any CSS unit as text ("9pt").

sheet = (
    TableSheet(simple, width_in=5)
    .style_table(
        font_size=12,
        text_align="center",
        header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"},
        corner_styles={"background-color": "#12275A"},
        index_styles={"background-color": "#F2F2F2", "font-weight": "normal", "text-align": "left"},
        data_styles={"border-bottom": "1px solid #E5E5E5"},
    )
    .format("{:.1%}")
    .panel(title="Performance by asset class")
)

Order of rules inside one call (the later one wins on the same property): (1) general arguments, (2) header_styles / index_styles / data_styles, (3) column_header_styles, (4) row_index_styles, (5) corner_styles.

Why the font size barely changes the image

With the default scale="uniform" the table is resized to fill its cell, so font_size mostly changes how heavy fixed-pixel borders look relative to the text. See scale.

Header and row heights

A row is as tall as its tallest cell. If you reduce the padding of the header cells, give corner_styles the same padding; if you reduce the data padding, reduce the index padding too: data_styles={"padding": "0.25em 0.6em"}, index_styles={"padding": "0.25em 0.6em"}.

docs.title: Number formats: format
docs.text:
format(formatter=None, subset=None, **kwargs) wraps Styler.format.

sheet.format("{:.1%}")                                    # every cell
sheet.format({"YTD": "{:.1%}", "1Y": "{:.1%}"})           # per column
sheet.format(lambda v: f"{v:+,.0f} bp", subset=["1M"])    # a function
sheet.format("{:.1f}", na_rep="-")                        # any Styler.format option

docs.title: Selected headers: column_header_styles
docs.text:
Each rule is a dictionary with "columns" (a label or a list), "styles" and an optional "level" (the header row; default is the last one, the row closest to the data).

sheet = (
    TableSheet(simple, width_in=5)
    .style_table(
        text_align="center",
        header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"},
        column_header_styles=[
            {"columns": ["YTD"], "styles": {"background-color": "#B7331F"}},
            {"columns": ["1Y", "3Y"], "styles": {"background-color": "#3075DB"}},
        ],
    )
    .format("{:.1%}")
)

docs.title: Selected index labels: row_index_styles
docs.text:
Each rule has "values" (a label or list), "level" (position, 0 = outermost, or the level name) and "styles". "parent" (a tuple of the outer-level values) restricts a repeated label to one section.

sheet = (
    TableSheet(multi, width_in=6)
    .style_table(
        font_size=11,
        text_align="center",
        header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A"},
        corner_styles={"background-color": "#12275A"},
        row_index_styles=[
            {"values": "Δ Yield", "level": 0, "styles": {"background-color": "#B7331F", "color": "white"}},
            {"values": "Δ Spreads", "level": 0, "styles": {"background-color": "#163A87", "color": "white"}},
            {"values": ["MTD", "YTD"], "level": 1, "parent": ("Δ Yield",), "styles": {"font-style": "italic"}},
            {"values": "AAA", "level": "Rating", "styles": {"color": "#B7331F"}},
        ],
        show_index_names=False,
    )
    .panel(title="MultiIndex table")
)

MultiIndex columns

With MultiIndex columns use complete tuples as labels (("Yield", "1M")). To style a group label of an upper level, use "level": 0 and list the group's columns starting with its first column (the one that carries the label).

Values that do not exist

A label that is not in the table matches nothing and is ignored silently.

docs.title: Table outline and header line
docs.text:
By default a table has no outline and a 1px black line under the column headers.

Method What it does table_border(width="1px", color="#cccccc", line_style="solid") Draws an outline. line_style="none" removes it. header_line(width="1px", color="black", line_style="solid") Style of the line between headers and data (line_style="none" removes it). 
sheet.table_border(color="#12275A")
sheet.header_line(color="#12275A", width=2)

Line thickness

The browser draws table borders in whole CSS pixels with a minimum of 1px ("0.5px" is drawn as 1px, "1.5px" as 1px). Because the sheet scales the table to fit its cell, the visible thickness is relative to the text: a 1px line is thinner next to a large font_size. To get thinner lines, increase font_size; to keep other sizes proportional use em units inside the table.

docs.title: Cells, rows and columns
docs.text:
These methods mirror the functional API. Labels are row index values and column names; for a MultiIndex use complete tuples.

Method Description style_cell(row, column, styles) CSS on one cell. style_cells(rows, columns, styles) CSS on every combination of the given rows and columns. border_cell(row, column, position="top", width="1px", color="black", line_style="solid") Border on one side of one cell. border_cells(rows, columns, position=..., ...) Border on one side of many cells. highlight_rows(rows, styles=None, include_index=True, index_level=None) Highlight whole rows. Default style: bold text and a 1px black box. highlight_columns(columns, styles=None, include_header=True, header_level=None) Highlight whole columns. border_rows(rows, position="bottom", styles=None) Horizontal line across the complete row (also across merged MultiIndex cells). styles accepts width, style (or line_style) and color. border_columns(columns, position="right", include_header=True, header_level=None, styles=None) Vertical line next to columns. 

sheet = (
    TableSheet(simple, width_in=5)
    .style_table(font_size=12, text_align="center")
    .format("{:.1%}")
    .highlight_rows("Total", styles={"background-color": "#FFF2CC"})
    .border_rows("Cash", position="bottom", styles={"width": "2px", "color": "#12275A"})
    .style_cell("Equity", "YTD", {"color": "#B7331F", "font-weight": "bold"})
    .border_columns("YTD", position="right", styles={"color": "#808080", "width": "1px"})
    .panel(title="Highlights and borders")
)

row_index_styles vs highlight_rows

row_index_styles paints only the index label. To style the data cells of a row use highlight_rows or style_cells.

docs.title: Conditional colors
docs.text:
text_color_by_range(ranges, subset=None) and background_color_by_range(ranges, subset=None) color each cell by the numeric interval it falls in. ranges is {(lower, upper): css_color}; the interval is lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive and the first match wins. subset limits the cells (use pd.IndexSlice for MultiIndex).

sheet = (
    TableSheet(multi, width_in=6)
    .style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center", show_index_names=False)
    .text_color_by_range({(-np.inf, 0): "#B7331F", (0, np.inf): "#1E8449"})
    .background_color_by_range({(25, np.inf): "#D9EAD3", (-np.inf, -20): "#F4CCCC"})
    .panel(title="Positive in green, negative in red")
)

docs.title: Any Styler operation: apply_styler
docs.text:
apply_styler(func, *args, **kwargs) runs any Styler method by name, or your own function func(styler, ...) -> Styler, and records it in the recipe:

sheet.apply_styler("background_gradient", cmap="Blues", axis=None)
sheet.apply_styler(lambda s: s.set_caption("Daily changes"))
sheet.apply_styler("hide", axis="columns", subset=["5Y"])

docs.title: Several tables, different styles
docs.text:
Use on(...) to choose which panels the next call affects. With no arguments it selects all panels:

sheet = (
    TableSheet({"yield": df_yield, "spreads": df_spreads}, width_in=12)
    .on().style_table(font_size=11, text_align="center")       # both
    .on("yield").format("{:+.0f}")                              # only yield
    .on("spreads").format("{:.1f}")                             # only spreads
)

See Panels, charts and layout.

docs.title: Inspecting and resetting styles
docs.text:
Method Description recipe (property) Dictionary {panel_name: [operation labels]} in the order they will be applied. Use it to debug the order of rules. clear_styles() Remove every recorded operation from the active tables. 

sheet = TableSheet(simple).style_table(font_size=11).format("{:.1%}").highlight_rows("Total")
sheet.recipe
Output

<bound method StylingMixin.recipe of TableSheet(panels=['panel_0'], active=['panel_0'], stacked, width_in=8.0)>

A wrong label fails immediately on the offending line (not when rendering), which makes mistakes easy to find.
