docs.title: Excel
docs.text:
The Excel module writes DataFrames to Excel workbooks in three situations:

Function Workbook state Engine Best for to_excel_open Open in Excel (live) xlwings Update a workbook you are looking at; models with formulas, charts and links that read the data. to_excel_closed Closed (a file on disk) openpyxl Automated jobs, servers, no Excel installed. Creates or updates a sheet of the file. to_excel_closed_styled Closed, new file pandas + openpyxl Export a styled table (Styler, see DfStyling). 
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.Excel.to_excel_closed(df, "report.xlsx", sheet="Data", cell="B2", to_table=True)

Requirements

to_excel_open needs Excel installed (Windows or macOS) and the xlwings package. The other two functions only need openpyxl. Because the package imports xlwings when the Excel module loads, xlwings must be installed in every environment (it is part of the package dependencies).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

dates = pd.bdate_range("2024-01-02", periods=5)
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"SPX": [4700.1, 4710.5, np.nan, 4725.0, 4731.2], "NDX": [16500.0, 16520.3, 16490.8, 16555.5, 16570.0]},
    index=pd.Index(dates, name="Date"),
)

docs.title: to_excel_closed
docs.text:
to_excel_closed(df, path, sheet="Hoja1", cell="A1", include_index=True, index_label=None, table_name="Tabla1", to_table=False, autofit=True, overwrite=True, table_style="TableStyleMedium2")

Writes the DataFrame into a workbook file. If the file does not exist it is created; if the sheet does not exist it is created; other sheets of an existing workbook are kept.

Parameter Default Description df DataFrame to write. path Workbook path (str or Path). sheet "Hoja1" Target sheet name. cell "A1" Top-left cell of the output (header row). include_index True Write the index as the first column(s). A MultiIndex becomes several columns. index_label None Header(s) for the index column(s): a string, or a list / tuple with one label per level for a MultiIndex. table_name "Tabla1" Name of the Excel table if to_table=True. to_table False Convert the written range to a formatted Excel table. An existing table with the same name is replaced. table_style "TableStyleMedium2" Style of the Excel table. autofit True Adjust column widths to the content (capped at 40 characters). overwrite True Clear the target range before writing. 

hp.Excel.to_excel_closed(df, "prices.xlsx", sheet="Prices", cell="B2", to_table=True, table_name="tbl_prices")

from openpyxl import load_workbook

ws = load_workbook("prices.xlsx")["Prices"]
[[c.value for c in row] for row in ws["B2:D4"]]
Output

[['Date', 'SPX', 'NDX'], [datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 2, 0, 0), 4700.1, 16500], [datetime.datetime(2024, 1, 3, 0, 0), 4710.5, 16520.3]]

Details to know:

  • The header row is written as text and centered; missing values (NaN, NaT, None) are written as empty cells.
  • Cells are written as values (no formulas). Dates are written as Excel dates.
  • Calling it again with the same sheet and cell refreshes the data; with overwrite=False existing cell values outside the new data are not cleared.
  • The workbook must not be open in Excel (Windows locks the file and PermissionError is raised).

docs.title: Several DataFrames in one workbook
docs.text:
Call it once per DataFrame, changing sheet and / or cell:

returns = df.pct_change().dropna()

hp.Excel.to_excel_closed(df, "report.xlsx", sheet="Prices")
hp.Excel.to_excel_closed(returns, "report.xlsx", sheet="Returns", index_label="Date")
hp.Excel.to_excel_closed(df.describe(), "report.xlsx", sheet="Summary", cell="A1")

load_workbook("report.xlsx").sheetnames
Output

['Sheet', 'Prices', 'Returns', 'Summary']

The default sheet name

The default sheet="Hoja1" (Spanish for Sheet1) and table_name="Tabla1" are only defaults: pass your own names. A freshly created workbook also contains its initial empty sheet (Sheet).

docs.title: to_excel_closed_styled
docs.text:
to_excel_closed_styled(styled_df, output_path, sheet_name="Sheet1", freeze_panes="B2", autofit=True, index=True)

Exports a Styler (or a plain DataFrame) to a new workbook, keeping the styles pandas can translate to Excel (colors, bold / italic, borders, alignment). Unlike to_excel_closed it always creates a new file (an existing file with the same name is overwritten).

Parameter Default Description styled_df Styler (from df.style or hp.DfStyling) or DataFrame. output_path Output .xlsx path. sheet_name "Sheet1" Sheet name. freeze_panes "B2" Cell where panes are frozen (header row and index column stay visible). None disables it. autofit True Adjust column widths (capped at 40). index True Export the index. 

import os

styled = hp.DfStyling.style_table(
    df.round(1),
    header_styles={"color": "white", "background-color": "#12275A", "font-weight": "bold"},
)
styled = hp.DfStyling.highlight_rows(styled, df.index[-1], include_index=False)

hp.Excel.to_excel_closed_styled(styled, "styled.xlsx", sheet_name="Prices", freeze_panes="B2")
os.path.exists("styled.xlsx")
Output

True

What survives the export

Excel understands a subset of CSS: background and text colors, font weight and style, borders and alignment are translated; layout properties (padding, font-family lists, etc.) are not. Check the result in Excel and keep the sheet-based image output (TableSheet) for pixel-exact looks.

docs.title: to_excel_open
docs.text:
to_excel_open(df, book, sheet="Hoja1", cell="A1", include_index=True, include_header=True, table_name="Tabla1", to_table=False, clear_range=False, **kwargs)

Writes the DataFrame into a workbook that is open in Excel, through xlwings. Nothing is saved to disk; the user (or your code) saves the workbook.

Parameter Default Description df DataFrame to write. book An xlwings.Book object, or a workbook name / path (str) that xlwings can find. Any other type raises TypeError. sheet "Hoja1" Sheet to write to. It is created if it does not exist. cell "A1" Top-left cell. include_index, include_header True, True Write the index / the column names. to_table False Convert the range to an Excel table (table_name). If the table already exists, it is resized to the new range. table_name "Tabla1" Name of the table. clear_range False Clear the current region around cell before writing (use it when the new data may be smaller than the previous one). **kwargs Extra arguments for ws.tables.add(...) of xlwings (for example table_style_name="TableStyleMedium2"). 
import xlwings as xw

wb = xw.Book("model.xlsx")                       # or xw.books.active

hp.Excel.to_excel_open(
    df,
    book=wb,
    sheet="Data",
    cell="A1",
    clear_range=True,
    to_table=True,
    table_name="tbl_prices",
)

Using the workbook name is equivalent when it is already open:

hp.Excel.to_excel_open(df, "model.xlsx", sheet="Data")

Typical pattern

Keep the formulas and charts of a model in an Excel template that reads from tables (tbl_prices). Refresh the data from Python with to_excel_open(..., to_table=True, clear_range=True); the tables resize and the formulas update.

docs.title: Choosing the right function
docs.text:
I want to... Use Refresh data inside an Excel model that is open to_excel_open Produce or update a data file in a job / server to_excel_closed Deliver a formatted table to a colleague to_excel_closed_styled Deliver a table as an image or put it in a slide TableSheet

API reference of Excel

docs.title: Annotations: tags, dots and shaded regions
docs.text:
Annotations add emphasis and explanation on top of a chart. There are two ways to use them:

  1. Declared inside a series (tags in graph_line, tag in graph_bar, graph_box_whiskers and graph_dist). The y-value is looked up for you: this is the recommended way for "last value", "peak" or "a given date".
  2. Free-standing methods (tag(), dot(), shade_x(), shade_y()) when you know the exact coordinates.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

docs.title: Tags declared inside a line series
docs.text:
In graph_line, each series accepts a tags list. Each item is one group of annotations:

Key Default Description x_values required "last", one x value or a list of x values (dates as strings or Timestamp, numbers, categories). show "tag_dot" "tag" (text only), "dot" (marker only) or "tag_dot". template "{ticker}\n{x_value:%b-%Y}: {y_value:,.2f}" Text, formatted with {ticker}, {label}, {x_value}, {y_value}. tag {} Style of the text: arguments of tag() (ubic_etq, fontsize, fontweight, font_color, bg_color, edge_color, show_bbox...). font_color defaults to the series color. dot {} Style of the marker: arguments of dot() (color, size, zorder...). color defaults to the series color. legend_label None Adds a legend entry for the markers.

docs.title: Last value
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[
        {
            "ticker": "SPX",
            "label": "S&P 500",
            "tags": [{
                "x_values": "last",
                "template": "{label}\n{y_value:,.1f}",
                "tag": {"ubic_etq": (-22, 16), "fontweight": "bold"},
            }],
        },
        {
            "ticker": "NDX",
            "label": "Nasdaq 100",
            "tags": [{
                "x_values": "last",
                "template": "{y_value:,.1f}",
                "tag": {"ubic_etq": (0, -16)},
            }],
        },
    ])
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Several points, with a legend entry
docs.text:
The y-values of the dates are read from the DataFrame. Pass pd.Timestamp objects when the template formats the date ({x_value:%b-%y}); a date string works to locate the point, but it stays a string and cannot be formatted as a date.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[
        {
            "ticker": "SPX",
            "color": "#12275A",
            "tags": [
                {
                    "x_values": [pd.Timestamp("2023-06-30"), pd.Timestamp("2024-03-28"), pd.Timestamp("2024-09-30")],
                    "show": "tag_dot",
                    "template": "{x_value:%b-%y}\n{y_value:,.0f}",
                    "dot": {"color": "#B7331F", "size": 40, "zorder": 8},
                    "tag": {"ubic_etq": (0, 16), "bg_color": "white", "edge_color": "#D9D9D9", "show_bbox": True},
                    "legend_label": "Rebalancing dates",
                },
            ],
        },
    ])
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Dots only
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[
        {"ticker": "AGG", "tags": [{"x_values": "last", "show": "dot", "dot": {"size": 50, "color": "#B7331F"}}]},
    ])
)

Tags in other charts

Bars: tag (value labels, centered tags, stack totals). Boxes: tag (last observation, statistics). Distributions: tag (last value, percentiles, literal values).

docs.title: tag()
docs.text:
Writes a text at the coordinate (x_value, y_value), optionally inside a rounded box.

Parameter Default Description x_value, y_value required Coordinate. For date axes pass a date (string or Timestamp); for bar charts with categories pass the position 0, 1, 2.... label required Text (\n for line breaks). ubic_etq (0, 17) Offset (dx, dy) in points from the coordinate. label_h_align, label_v_align "center", "center" Alignment relative to the anchor. fontsize, fontweight, font_color 7, "normal", "black" Text style. show_bbox False Draw a rounded box behind the text. bg_color, bg_alpha, edge_color "#ECEFF1", 1.0, "none" Box style. text_edge_color, text_edge_width None, 0.0 Outline around the letters (readability on busy charts). zorder 6 Drawing order. 

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}])
    .tag(
        x_value="2024-03-28",
        y_value=prices.loc["2024-03-28", "SPX"],
        label="Rate cut\nexpectations",
        ubic_etq=(-45, 25),
        show_bbox=True,
        bg_color="white",
        edge_color="#B7331F",
        font_color="#B7331F",
    )
    .dot(x_value="2024-03-28", y_value=prices.loc["2024-03-28", "SPX"], color="#B7331F", size=45)
)

docs.title: dot()
docs.text:
Draws a marker (a scatter point) at a coordinate.

Parameter Default Description x_value, y_value required Coordinate. color "red" Fill color (marker_color overrides it). size 30 Marker area (points²). markersize sets the diameter instead. marker "o" Matplotlib marker style ("s", "^", "D"...). marker_edgecolor, marker_edgewidth None, 0.0 Edge. alpha, zorder, clip_on 1.0, 5, True Opacity, drawing order, clipping. label, legend None, True Legend text; if label is given the dot is added to the legend. 
g.dot(x_value="2024-12-27", y_value=120.0, marker="^", color="green", size=60, label="Buy signal")

docs.title: shade_x(): shaded periods
docs.text:
Shades one or more x ranges across the full height of the axis: recessions, rate-hiking cycles, events, investment periods.

periods can be a single (start, end) tuple, a list of tuples, or a list of dictionaries with their own color, alpha, label and hatch.

Parameter Default Description periods required (start, end), [(start, end), ...] or [{"start", "end", "color", "alpha", "label", "hatch"}, ...]. color, alpha "#B0B0B0", 0.25 Default fill. label None Legend label (shown once). hatch None Hatch pattern, e.g. "//". ymin, ymax 0.0, 1.0 Vertical extent, as fractions of the axis. zorder 0 Drawing order. clip_to_xlim True Do not extend the axis. 

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}, {"ticker": "NDX"}])
    .shade_x(
        [
            {"start": "2023-03-01", "end": "2023-06-30", "color": "#B7331F", "alpha": 0.15, "label": "Stress period"},
            {"start": "2024-08-01", "end": "2024-10-31", "color": "#3075DB", "alpha": 0.15, "label": "Recovery"},
        ]
    )
    .add_legend()
)

For recessions there is a ready-made helper: add_recessions().

docs.title: shade_y(): shaded bands
docs.text:
Shades a horizontal band between two y values: target ranges, risk zones, valuation bands.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "AGG"}])
    .shade_y((102, 106), color="#3075DB", alpha=0.12, label="Target range")
    .add_legend()
)

Parameter Default Description period required (lower, upper) y values. color, alpha, zorder, label, hatch as shade_x Style. xmin, xmax 0.0, 1.0 Horizontal extent, as fractions of the axis. clip_to_ylim True Do not extend the axis.

docs.title: Which axis do annotations use?
docs.text:
Annotations go to the active subplot (axis(i)) and, for charts with two y axes, the series tags of a "right" series are drawn on the right axis automatically.

API reference of annotations

docs.title: Axes
docs.text:
Every chart method takes an x_axis argument to format the x-axis, and the method config_yaxis() formats the y-axes (left and right). get_axis() gives you the raw Matplotlib axis for anything not covered.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

docs.title: X axis
docs.text:
x_axis is a dictionary (or an XAxisConfig). The method that interprets it is prep_x_axis() (see the API reference), which looks at the type of the index and picks one of four modes:

Index Mode What you get DatetimeIndex datetime A real time axis. Ticks every tick_step months, labels formatted with fmt (default %b-%y). Weekends are visible as gaps. DatetimeIndex + bbg_format=True bbg Bloomberg-style: one position per observation (no gaps), month labels with the year below. tick_step counts months. Numeric index numeric Ticks every tick_step observations, labels with fmt (default ",.0f"). Anything else (text) categorical One position per category, ticks every tick_step categories.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Key Default Description bbg_format False Bloomberg-style axis (dates only). tick_step 6 Spacing of ticks (see the table above for the unit of each mode). Must be a positive integer. fmt None Format of the labels: strftime for dates ("%b-%y", "%Y"), a format spec for numbers (",.0f", ".1%"). lim None (start, end) tuple. Filters the rows of the DataFrame before drawing. Either side can be None. tick_values None Explicit positions of the ticks. Dates, numbers or category names (or positions). tick_labels None Text of each tick (same length as tick_values). tick_label_map None Dictionary to rename some labels: {"Jan-24": "Start"}. fontsize 8 Label size. rotation, ha, va 0, "center", "top" Label rotation and alignment. label_color None Label color. show_years True Year labels under a Bloomberg-style axis. year_y_offset -0.08 Vertical position of those year labels.

docs.title: Regular time axis
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}], x_axis={"fmt": "%b-%y", "tick_step": 3, "rotation": 45, "ha": "right"})
    .add_title("Ticks every 3 months")
)

docs.title: Bloomberg-style axis
docs.text:
Removes the gaps of non-trading days and prints each year centered below its months. Month names are Spanish abbreviations unless fmt is given.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}], x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 3})
    .add_title("Bloomberg-style axis")
)

docs.title: Restrict the period
docs.text:
lim removes rows outside the range, so all charts and tags use only that period:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(
        series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}, {"ticker": "NDX"}],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1, "lim": ("2024-06-01", None)},
    )
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Custom ticks and labels
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(
        series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}],
        x_axis={
            "tick_values": ["2023-01-02", "2024-01-02", "2024-12-27"],
            "tick_labels": ["Start", "One year", "Today"],
        },
    )
)

docs.title: Categorical axis
docs.text:
For text indexes the ticks are positions (tick_step=6 by default, so use 1 to show every category). tick_label_map renames individual labels:

by_country = pd.DataFrame(
    {"P/E": [20.5, 13.1, 22.8, 15.4]},
    index=["US", "Europe", "Japan", "EM"],
)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(by_country)
    .graph_bar(x_axis={"tick_step": 1, "tick_label_map": {"US": "United States", "EM": "Emerging"}})
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".1f")
)

Box plots and pies

graph_box_whiskers() reads fontsize, rotation, ha, va, label_color, tick_labels and tick_label_map from x_axis to format the names under each box. graph_dist() reads fmt, tick_values, tick_labels, lim... for its numeric axis (see Distribution). graph_pie() has no x-axis.

docs.title: Y axes: config_yaxis
docs.text:
config_yaxis() acts on the left axis by default or on the right axis with side="right". Calls can be chained: each one configures one side.

Parameter Default Description lim None (min, max) of the axis. fmt None Number format of the ticks: ",.0f", ".1%", ",.2f". fontsize 7 Tick label size. tick_step None Fixed spacing between ticks (in axis units). label, label_fontsize, label_color None Axis title and its style. tick_color, spine_color None Colors of the ticks and of the axis line. margins_x 0.01 Horizontal margin around the data. side None (left) "left" or "right". ax None A specific Matplotlib axis.

docs.title: Two axes
docs.text:
Give each series its axis_side and format each side separately:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[
        {"ticker": "SPX", "label": "S&P 500 (left)", "axis_side": "left", "color": "#12275A"},
        {"ticker": "AGG", "label": "Aggregate bond (right)", "axis_side": "right", "color": "#B7331F"},
    ])
    .config_yaxis(side="left", fmt=",.0f", label="Equity", label_color="#12275A", spine_color="#12275A", tick_color="#12275A")
    .config_yaxis(side="right", fmt=",.1f", label="Bonds", label_color="#B7331F", spine_color="#B7331F", tick_color="#B7331F")
    .add_legend()
)

Right-axis legend

add_legend() merges the entries of both axes (include_right_axis=True).

docs.title: Axis limits and tick spacing
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "AGG"}])
    .config_yaxis(lim=(90, 115), tick_step=5, fmt=",.0f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
)

docs.title: The raw Matplotlib axis
docs.text:
get_axis(side="left") returns the matplotlib.axes.Axes of the active subplot ("right" returns the secondary axis if the chart has one). Use it for anything the API does not cover:

ax = g.get_axis()
ax.set_ylabel("Index level")
ax.annotate("Rate hike", xy=(pd.Timestamp("2024-03-20"), 105), xytext=(10, 20), textcoords="offset points")

The complete figure is available with g.show() (see Export).

docs.title: Selecting the active subplot
docs.text: In a multi-panel figure, axis(i) selects the subplot where the next chart / decoration goes (0 = top-left, counting row by row). See Plotting.

docs.title: Export, reuse and chaining
docs.text:
Once a chart is built you can display it, get the Matplotlib Figure, save a PNG file or keep the image in memory (a BytesIO buffer) to insert it later in a PowerPoint, a Word report or a TableSheet.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

def build():
    return (
        hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
        .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}])
        .add_title("S&P 500")
    )

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Method Returns Use it for show() matplotlib.figure.Figure Display in a notebook or get the figure for further Matplotlib work. The chart stays editable. save() io.BytesIO (or None if dir is given) In-memory PNG, ready for PowerPoint / Word / other libraries. Closes the figure. render(name, dir) None Write <dir>/<name>.png to disk. Closes the figure. render_from_dict(images) None Display and save a whole dictionary of buffers (from helpers_ps.MtpltGraph import render_from_dict).

docs.title: show()
docs.text:
Returns the figure. In a notebook the figure is displayed automatically; in a script you decide what to do with it:

fig = build().show()
fig.savefig("chart.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")   # any Matplotlib option

show() raises RuntimeError("Plot must exist") if no chart has been created.

docs.title: save(): PNG in memory
docs.text:
save() renders the figure into a BytesIO object (PNG, dpi=400 by default), closes it and resets the internal state, so the same GraphMtplt object can be reused for another chart.

buffer = build().save(dpi=200)
type(buffer).__name__, len(buffer.getvalue()) > 10_000
Output

('BytesIO', True)

docs.title: Collect many charts in a dictionary
docs.text:
Pass a dictionary with dir= and a name; the buffer is stored as dir[name] and the method returns None. This is the standard way to prepare all the charts of a report:

images = {}

build().save(dir=images, name="spx")
(
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "AGG"}])
    .add_title("Aggregate bond")
    .save(dir=images, name="agg")
)

list(images)
Output

['spx', 'agg']

The module also provides a shared registry, helpers_ps.MtpltGraph.config.buffers, that you can use as dir=buffers when several notebooks / functions need to share images:

from helpers_ps.MtpltGraph.config import buffers

build().save(dir=buffers, name="spx")

docs.title: Reading the buffer
docs.text:
from PIL import Image
image = Image.open(buffer)         # buffer.seek(0) if it was already read

with open("chart.png", "wb") as file:
    file.write(buffer.getvalue())

docs.title: render(): PNG on disk
docs.text:
render(name, dir, dpi=400) writes <dir>/<name>.png. The folder must exist.

import os

os.makedirs("charts", exist_ok=True)
build().render(name="spx", dir="charts", dpi=300)
os.listdir("charts")
Output

['spx.png']

docs.title: render_from_dict(): preview and save a dictionary of buffers
docs.text:
Displays every buffer of a dictionary with Matplotlib and writes them to output_dir (created if missing):

from helpers_ps.MtpltGraph import render_from_dict

render_from_dict(images, output_dir="saved_plots", figsize=(6, 4))

docs.title: Figure size and resolution
docs.text:
The figure size is set when the canvas is created, with plot(figsize=(width, height)) in inches (default (6.0, 4.8)). dpi in save() / render() controls the pixel resolution of the export:

Target Suggestion Slide with one chart plot(figsize=(6, 4.8)), dpi=400 (default) Wide chart plot(figsize=(10, 4)) Quick preview dpi=100

Fixed-size canvas + a different layout

Titles, subtitles and the source are placed with figure coordinates (x=0.02, y=0.93...), so they keep their position when you change figsize. Fine-tune with subplot_adjust(left=..., right=..., top=..., bottom=...) (see Plotting).

docs.title: Chaining helpers: pipe() and tap()
docs.text:
Both receive the graph object as first argument, which lets you package a style or a debug step in a reusable function without breaking the chain.

Method The function returns... The chain continues with... pipe(func, *args, **kwargs) a graph object, or None the returned object (or the same graph if None) tap(func, *args, **kwargs) ignored always the same graph 

def corporate_style(graph, title):
    """Reusable block: title, source and guides in one call."""
    return (
        graph
        .add_title(title)
        .add_source("Source: Bloomberg")
        .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
        .config_yaxis(fmt=",.0f")
    )

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}, {"ticker": "NDX"}])
    .pipe(corporate_style, title="Equity indices")
    .tap(lambda graph: print("series drawn:", [t[0] for t in graph._ticker_label_color]))
    .add_legend()
)

tap() is also the way to call methods that do not return the graph, such as add_recessions().

docs.title: Using the chart in other modules
docs.text: Destination How PowerPoint Save to a buffer and insert with python-pptx: slide.shapes.add_picture(buffer, left, top, width). For native (editable) charts use the Ppt module instead. Table sheet (TableSheet) sheet.add_image(g, name="curve") accepts the GraphMtplt object directly. See DfStyling: charts in a sheet. Excel Save to a file with render() and use openpyxl / xlsxwriter to insert the picture.

docs.title: GraphMtplt: Getting Started
docs.text:
GraphMtplt is the main charting class of Helpers PS. It builds institutional-style Matplotlib charts (consistent fonts, colors, title / subtitle / source blocks, tags and reference lines) from a plain pandas.DataFrame, using a fluent, chainable API.

import helpers_ps as hp

g = hp.GraphMtplt(df).graph_line().add_title("My first chart")

Every method returns the same GraphMtplt object, so a chart is normally written as one chained expression: create the object, add one or more charts, decorate, export.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text: Step What you do Main methods 1. Data Pass a DataFrame (or a list of them). The index is the x-axis and each column is a series. hp.GraphMtplt(df) 2. Canvas Optional. Create the figure and its grid of subplots. If you skip it, a single-plot figure is created automatically by the first chart method. .plot(), .axis(), .subplot_adjust() 3. Chart Draw one chart type on the active axis. .graph_line(), .graph_bar(), .graph_pie(), .graph_box_whiskers(), .graph_dist() 4. Decorate Titles, legend, axes formatting, tags, dots, shaded regions, reference lines. .add_title(), .add_legend(), .config_yaxis(), .tag(), .horizontal_lines() ... 5. Export Show it, get the Matplotlib figure, or save a PNG / an in-memory buffer. .show(), .save(), .render()

docs.title: Your first chart
docs.text:
First create some sample data. Every example of this documentation can be copied and pasted after this block.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()          # fonts and number formatting (see "Theme" below)

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)


prices.tail(3).round(2)
Output

               SPX     NDX     AGG
2024-12-25  120.57  102.20  104.37
2024-12-26  119.14  101.43  104.09
2024-12-27  120.02  102.57  104.05

A line chart with a title, a subtitle, a source line and a legend:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[
        {"ticker": "SPX", "label": "S&P 500"},
        {"ticker": "NDX", "label": "Nasdaq 100"},
    ])
    .add_title("Equity indices")
    .add_subtitle("Simulated prices (start = 100)")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
    .add_legend()
)

In a Jupyter notebook the figure is displayed automatically when the cell finishes. In a script, call .show() to get the matplotlib.figure.Figure or .save() / .render() to write a PNG (see Export).

Where do the series come from?

series is a list of one dictionary per column you want to draw. If you omit series, all columns are drawn with default colors. Keys such as label, color, axis_side or lw customize each series; they are documented in every chart page.

docs.title: Chart types
docs.text: Method Use it for Data layout Page graph_line() Time series, indices, yields, cumulative performance. index = dates (or numbers / categories), columns = series Line graph_bar() Simple, grouped or stacked bars: monthly returns, allocations, contributions. index = x (dates or categories), columns = series Bar graph_pie() Pie and donut: weights of a portfolio at one point in time. index = categories, one column of values Pie graph_box_whiskers() Historical distribution of each series (P/E, spreads, yields) with markers for the last observation. each column = one box Box & Whiskers graph_dist() Histogram with optional fitted / theoretical curves and highlighted references (VaR, last return, percentiles). each column = one distribution Distribution

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
Besides the chart methods there are ready-made blocks that work on any chart type.

Group Methods Page Figure and layout plot(), axis(), subplot_adjust(), add_title(), add_subtitle(), add_source(), add_plot_title() Plotting, Layout Axes x_axis={...} argument of every chart, config_yaxis(), get_axis() Axes Annotations tag(), dot(), shade_x(), shade_y() Annotations Legends and reference lines add_legend(), add_legend_point(), horizontal_lines(), vertical_lines(), horizontal_guides(), vertical_guides(), add_recessions() Legends and reference lines Export and chaining show(), save(), render(), pipe(), tap(), render_from_dict() Export

docs.title: Several DataFrames in one object
docs.text:
GraphMtplt accepts a single DataFrame or a list. Chart methods take df_index to pick which one to draw (default 0):

returns = prices.pct_change().dropna()
monthly = returns.resample("ME").apply(lambda r: (1 + r).prod() - 1)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt([prices, monthly])
    .plot(nrows=2, height_ratios=[3, 2], hspace=0.35)
    .axis(0).graph_line(df_index=0)
    .axis(1).graph_bar(
        df_index=1,
        series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}],
        x_axis={"fmt": "%b-%y", "tick_step": 3},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
)

docs.title: Series configuration: dictionaries or dataclasses
docs.text:
A series can be described with a plain dictionary (recommended, autocompletion-friendly in most editors thanks to TypedDict) or with the equivalent dataclass:

from helpers_ps.MtpltGraph.models import LineSeriesConfig

hp.GraphMtplt(prices).graph_line(series=[
    {"ticker": "SPX", "color": "#12275A", "lw": 2},          # dictionary
    LineSeriesConfig(ticker="NDX", color="#B7331F", lw=1.2), # dataclass
])

Invalid keys or values fail early with an explicit message (for example axis_side must be "left" or "right"). The available dataclasses are LineSeriesConfig, BarSeriesConfig, BoxSeriesConfig, DistSeriesConfig, DistCurveConfig and XAxisConfig, all importable from helpers_ps.MtpltGraph.models.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text:
hp.set_graph_theme() configures Matplotlib globally (font family, base font size, title size / weight and locale-aware number formatting). Call it once at the top of a notebook or script.

hp.set_graph_theme(
    font_family="Inter",          # default; falls back to a system font if not installed
    font_size=9,
    title_size=12,
    title_weight="bold",
    use_locale=True,              # decimal / thousand separators of the locale
    locale_name="es_ES.UTF-8",    # Windows: "Spanish_Spain.1252"
)

Font not found?

If you installed the Inter font after Matplotlib was imported, call hp.set_graph_theme(rebuild_font_cache=True) once. Use ignore_matplotlib_warnings=True to silence font warnings.

The default color palette is hp.PALETA_COLORES (a list of hex colors). Series without an explicit color take colors from it in order.

docs.title: Typical errors
docs.text: Message Cause Fix Ticker 'X' was not found in the selected DataFrame. The ticker of a series is not a column. Check df.columns. Duplicated tickers are not allowed in 'series'. The same column appears twice in series. Use one entry per column. Multiple bar series require grouped=True or stacked=True. graph_bar(grouped=False) with several series. Remove grouped=False or use stacked=True. No existe grafico para agregar las recesiones / ...no tiene como eje fechas add_recessions() before a chart, or on a non-date axis. Draw a time-series chart first. The title of a subplot disappears add_title() clears the title of the active axis. Call add_title() before add_plot_title(). Few labels on the x-axis of a bar chart Default tick_step is 6. Use x_axis={"tick_step": 1}. See Axes.

docs.title: Legends, guides and reference lines
docs.text:
This page covers the elements that help to read a chart: legends, grid guides, reference levels, event lines and recession shading. All of them work on any chart that has an x-axis and can be chained after the chart method.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

docs.title: Legends
docs.text:
add_legend() collects the labels of everything drawn on the active axis and on its right axis, plus any custom entries registered with add_legend_point(), removes duplicates and draws one legend.

Parameter Default Description loc "upper left" Matplotlib location. bbox_to_anchor None Anchor to place the legend outside the plot, e.g. (0.5, -0.12). ncol 1 Number of columns. fontsize 7 Text size. frameon, edgecolor, facecolor, framealpha True, "white", "white", 0.6 Frame. include_right_axis True Also list the series of the right axis. legend_mode "all" "all" (default), "series" or "points" (only the custom markers registered through dot(label=...) / add_legend_point()).

The text of each entry is the label of the series (the column name if omitted).

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[
        {"ticker": "SPX", "label": "S&P 500"},
        {"ticker": "NDX", "label": "Nasdaq 100"},
        {"ticker": "AGG", "label": "Global Aggregate", "axis_side": "right", "color": "#B7331F"},
    ])
    .add_legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.12), ncol=3)
    .add_title("Legend above the plot")
)

docs.title: Custom legend points
docs.text:
add_legend_point() adds an entry without plotting anything: useful for events, signals or markers drawn with dot().

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}])
    .dot(x_value="2024-03-28", y_value=float(prices.loc["2024-03-28", "SPX"]), color="#B7331F", size=45)
    .add_legend_point(label="Policy meeting", color="#B7331F", marker="o", markersize=6)
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Guides (grid lines)
docs.text:
Guides are the light dashed grid lines that make values easier to read.

Method What it does Main options horizontal_guides() Horizontal grid on the left, right or both y-axes, with an emphasized zero line. side ("left", "right", "both"), mostrar_cero, linestyle, linewidth, color, alpha, zero_color, zero_linewidth... vertical_guides() Vertical grid on the x-axis. linestyle, linewidth, color, alpha. 

returns = prices.pct_change().dropna().resample("ME").apply(lambda r: (1 + r).prod() - 1)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_bar(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}], x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 2})
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides(zero_color="black", zero_linewidth=1.2)
    .vertical_guides()
)

Guides and the right axis

With two y-axes use horizontal_guides(side="both") to draw guides for both, or choose the side whose scale you want the grid to follow.

docs.title: Reference lines
docs.text: Reference lines mark levels (targets, thresholds, averages) and events (dates).

docs.title: horizontal_lines()
docs.text: Parameter Default Description y_values required One value or a list. side "left" Axis whose scale the values refer to ("left" / "right"). color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha "gray", None, 0.5, 1.0 Style. label None Legend label (applied to the first line). zorder 4 Drawing order.

docs.title: vertical_lines()
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description x_values required One x value or a list (dates, numbers, categories). labels None Legend label(s): a string or a list (one per line). color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha "gray", None, 0.5, 1.0 Style. ymin, ymax 0.0, 1.0 Vertical extent as a fraction of the axis. zorder 4 Drawing order. 

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX", "label": "S&P 500"}])
    .horizontal_lines([100], color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    .horizontal_lines([115], color="#B7331F", linestyle="--", label="Target")
    .vertical_lines(["2023-09-29", "2024-06-28"], color="#3075DB", linestyle=":", linewidth=1, labels="Rebalancing")
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Recessions
docs.text:
add_recessions() shades recession periods from the database bundled with the package (helpers_ps/Data/recessions.csv). Available countries: "United States" (default) and "Peru". It only works on date axes (datetime or Bloomberg-style).

monthly_idx = pd.date_range("2000-01-31", "2024-12-31", freq="ME")
long_history = pd.DataFrame(
    {"SPX": 100 * np.exp(np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.006, 0.04, len(monthly_idx))))},
    index=monthly_idx,
)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(long_history)
    .graph_line(series=[{"ticker": "SPX"}], x_axis={"tick_step": 36, "fmt": "%Y"})
    .tap(lambda graph: graph.add_recessions(controles={"color": "grey", "alpha": 0.25, "label": "US recession"}))
    .add_legend()
)

add_recessions() ends the chain

When it draws, add_recessions() returns None instead of the graph object, so a method chained after it fails. Either call it last, or wrap it in tap() as above (tap runs a function and keeps the chain alive). Other countries: graph.add_recessions(country="Peru").

controles is passed to shade_x(): color, alpha, hatch, label, zorder. The default is gray with alpha=0.3.

To read the data without drawing:

recessions = hp.GraphMtplt().add_recessions(data_frame=True)
recessions.query("country == 'Peru'").tail(3)
Output

            country start_date   end_date     description
recesion_id                                              
34             Peru 1998-01-01 1999-12-31  Asia + El Niño
35             Peru 2009-01-01 2009-12-31   Crisis global
36             Peru 2020-03-01 2020-12-31     COVID shock

Order matters

Call add_recessions() after the chart method: it needs the axis mode and limits that the chart creates. On non-date axes it raises TypeError; for countries without data, NotImplementedError.

API reference of legends and reference lines

docs.title: Bar chart: graph_bar
docs.text:
graph_bar() draws simple, grouped or stacked bars on the active axis. The x-axis can be time (the index is a DatetimeIndex) or categorical (the index holds names such as "Equity", "Bonds").

Layout How to get it Simple bars one series Grouped bars (side by side) several series (default) or grouped=True Stacked bars stacked=True

docs.title: Expected DataFrame
docs.text:
The index is the x-axis and every column is a series. For the examples of this page:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# Monthly returns: index = month-end dates
monthly = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Portfolio": rng.normal(0.010, 0.020, 12),
        "Benchmark": rng.normal(0.008, 0.018, 12),
    },
    index=pd.date_range("2024-01-31", periods=12, freq="ME"),
)

# Asset allocation: index = categories
alloc = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Equity": [0.30, 0.50, 0.70],
        "Bonds": [0.60, 0.40, 0.25],
        "Cash": [0.10, 0.10, 0.05],
    },
    index=["Conservative", "Balanced", "Growth"],
)


monthly.head(3).round(4)
Output

            Portfolio  Benchmark
2024-01-31     0.0100     0.0099
2024-02-29     0.0160    -0.0087
2024-03-31     0.0045     0.0075

docs.title: Simple bars
docs.text:
With one series nothing else is needed. For monthly data use x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1}: every bar gets its own position and its month label (the default tick_step is 6, which would label only every sixth month):

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(monthly)
    .graph_bar(
        series=[{"ticker": "Portfolio", "label": "Portfolio"}],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides()
    .add_title("Monthly return")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

Colors

If color is omitted, each series takes the next color of the palette hp.PALETA_COLORES. Set it explicitly with {"ticker": "Portfolio", "color": "#12275A"}.

docs.title: Grouped bars
docs.text:
When there are two or more series and neither stacked nor grouped is given, the bars are grouped automatically:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(monthly)
    .graph_bar(
        series=[
            {"ticker": "Portfolio", "color": "#12275A"},
            {"ticker": "Benchmark", "color": "#B7331F"},
        ],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides()
    .add_legend(ncol=2)
    .add_title("Portfolio vs benchmark")
)

bar_width (0-1, default 0.8) controls the width of the whole group and alpha (default 0.95) the opacity.

docs.title: Stacked bars
docs.text:
stacked=True stacks the series in the order of series. Positive and negative values are stacked separately (positives above zero, negatives below), so mixed-sign contributions work.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(alloc)
    .graph_bar(
        stacked=True,
        series=[
            {"ticker": "Equity", "label": "Equities"},
            {"ticker": "Bonds", "label": "Fixed income"},
            {"ticker": "Cash", "label": "Cash"},
        ],
        x_axis={"tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .add_legend(ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.1))
    .add_title("Strategic allocation by profile")
)

Categorical axes and tick_step

On a categorical axis the default tick_step=6 would print one label every six categories. Use x_axis={"tick_step": 1} to show them all.

docs.title: Bars on the right axis
docs.text: Each series has its own axis_side ("left" or "right"). Grouped bars can mix both axes; stacked bars cannot (ValueError).

docs.title: Tags on bars
docs.text:
Each series accepts a tag list. Every item draws labels on selected bars. Three modes are available through show:

show Where the label goes Template fields "value_label" (default) Above the bar end (below for negatives). On stacked bars: centered in the segment. {y_value} "bar_tag" Centered inside the bar. {y_value} "stack_total" Above the whole stack. {total_value}

All modes also support {ticker}, {label} and {x_value}. Other keys of a tag item:

Key Default Description x_values "last" "last", "all", one index value or a list of index values (dates or category names). template "{y_value:,.2f}" Python format string. ubic_etq automatic Offset (x, y) in points from the anchor. fontsize, color, fontweight, fontstyle, rotation, alpha 8, #262626, normal... Text style. bbox, arrowprops none Matplotlib bbox / arrow dictionaries. zorder, clip_on, label_h_align, label_v_align 5, False Drawing order, clipping, alignment.

docs.title: Value labels on all bars
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(monthly)
    .graph_bar(
        series=[{
            "ticker": "Portfolio",
            "tag": [{"x_values": "all", "template": "{y_value:.1%}", "fontsize": 6}],
        }],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides()
    .add_title("Monthly return of the portfolio")
)

docs.title: Only some bars
docs.text:
x_values accepts index values. With a DatetimeIndex pass pd.Timestamp objects (date strings are only matched against a text / categorical index), and use "last" or "all" as a standalone value, not inside a list. To combine both, use two tag items:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(monthly)
    .graph_bar(
        series=[{
            "ticker": "Portfolio",
            "tag": [
                {"x_values": [pd.Timestamp("2024-03-31")], "template": "{x_value:%b}: {y_value:.1%}"},
                {"x_values": "last", "template": "Last: {y_value:.1%}"},
            ],
        }],
        x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%")
    .horizontal_guides()
)

docs.title: Centered tags and stack totals
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(alloc)
    .graph_bar(
        stacked=True,
        series=[
            {"ticker": "Equity", "label": "Equities", "color": "#12275A",
             "tag": [{"show": "bar_tag", "x_values": "all", "template": "{y_value:.0%}", "color": "white"}]},
            {"ticker": "Bonds", "label": "Fixed income", "color": "#3075DB",
             "tag": [{"show": "bar_tag", "x_values": "all", "template": "{y_value:.0%}", "color": "white"}]},
            {"ticker": "Cash", "label": "Cash", "color": "#B7331F",
             "tag": [{"show": "stack_total", "x_values": "all", "template": "Total {total_value:.0%}"}]},
        ],
        x_axis={"tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0%", lim=(0, 1.15))
    .add_legend(ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.12))
)

Where to declare stack_total

A stack total is the same for every series, so declare it on one series (usually the last one) to draw it only once.

docs.title: Daily data: Bloomberg-style axis
docs.text:
With a daily DatetimeIndex, x_axis={"bbg_format": True} removes the gaps of weekends and holidays (one position per observation) and prints month abbreviations with the year below, like a Bloomberg terminal. Bars and tags use the same positions.

Month names

In Bloomberg-style axes the default month labels are Spanish abbreviations (Ene, Abr, Ago, Dic). Pass fmt="%b-%y" (or another strftime format) to use the language of the active locale instead.

daily = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Daily return": rng.normal(0.0004, 0.01, 60)},
    index=pd.bdate_range("2024-09-02", periods=60),
)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(daily)
    .graph_bar(x_axis={"bbg_format": True, "tick_step": 1})
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".1%")
    .horizontal_guides()
    .add_title("Daily returns")
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description series all columns List of dictionaries / BarSeriesConfig: ticker, label, color, axis_side ("left"/"right"), tag. df_index 0 Which DataFrame of the object to use. grouped None None = automatic (grouped if there are 2+ series and stacked is False). stacked False Stack the series. Cannot be combined with grouped=True. bar_width 0.8 Width as a fraction of the spacing between observations (0 < w <= 1). alpha 0.95 Opacity. x_axis None X-axis settings, see Axes.

Full signature: API reference.

docs.title: Typical use cases
docs.text:
• Asset allocation by profile (stacked).
  • Return contribution or attribution by asset class (stacked, with negatives).
  • Monthly / yearly returns, portfolio vs benchmark (grouped).
  • Country, sector or currency distribution (categorical).

docs.title: Box & Whiskers: graph_box_whiskers
docs.text: graph_box_whiskers() draws one box per column to show the historical distribution of each series: median, quartiles and range. It is typically used for relative valuation (P/E, EV/EBITDA), yields or spreads, adding a marker for the last observation so you can see where today sits within its own history.

docs.title: Expected DataFrame
docs.text:
Every column is a series (one box). The index is only used to locate observations when you want to highlight one (for example the last date).

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

dates = pd.bdate_range("2015-01-01", periods=2500)

def ar1(mean, sd, n, phi=0.995):
    """Mean-reverting series, similar to a valuation multiple."""
    x = np.empty(n)
    x[0] = mean
    for t in range(1, n):
        x[t] = mean + phi * (x[t - 1] - mean) + rng.normal(0, sd)
    return x

pe = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "SPX": ar1(19, 0.25, len(dates)),
        "NDX": ar1(25, 0.35, len(dates)),
        "SX5E": ar1(14, 0.15, len(dates)),
        "MXEF": ar1(12, 0.12, len(dates)),
    },
    index=dates,
)


pe.describe().round(1).loc[["min", "25%", "50%", "75%", "max"]]
Output

      SPX   NDX  SX5E  MXEF
min  14.6  19.3  11.3   9.6
25%  18.2  23.8  14.0  11.5
50%  19.6  25.4  14.7  12.1
75%  20.5  27.3  15.8  12.6
max  23.3  35.3  19.0  14.6

docs.title: Basic example
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(pe)
    .graph_box_whiskers()
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .add_title("Historical P/E")
    .add_subtitle("Whiskers: minimum and maximum since 2015")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

By default the whiskers reach the minimum and maximum (whis=(0, 100)) and outliers are not drawn. To use the classic 1.5 x IQR rule pass box_config={"whis": 1.5, "showfliers": True}.

docs.title: Labels, colors and a subset of series
docs.text:
series selects the columns, their order, display names and colors:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(pe)
    .graph_box_whiskers(
        series=[
            {"ticker": "SPX", "label": "S&P 500", "color": "#12275A"},
            {"ticker": "SX5E", "label": "Euro Stoxx 50", "color": "#3075DB"},
            {"ticker": "MXEF", "label": "MSCI EM", "color": "#B7331F"},
        ],
        box_face_alpha=0.6,
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
)

docs.title: Highlight the last observation
docs.text:
Each series takes a tag list. Every item of the list is a reference made of:

  • x_values: which observations of the DataFrame ("last", "all", an index value or a list of them),
  • dot: the marker (arguments of dot()),
  • tag: the text label (arguments of tag()); its text template goes in the key label.

Set dot or tag to None (or omit it) to draw only the other element.

def last_value(ticker, label, color="#B7331F"):
    return {
        "ticker": ticker,
        "label": label,
        "tag": [{
            "x_values": "last",
            "dot": {"color": color, "size": 40, "zorder": 8},
            "tag": {
                "label": "{y_value:.1f}x",
                "ubic_etq": (22, 0),
                "fontsize": 7,
                "bg_color": "white",
                "edge_color": "#D9D9D9",
                "show_bbox": True,
            },
        }],
    }

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(pe)
    .graph_box_whiskers(series=[
        last_value("SPX", "S&P 500"),
        last_value("NDX", "Nasdaq 100"),
        last_value("SX5E", "Euro Stoxx 50"),
        last_value("MXEF", "MSCI EM"),
    ])
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .add_title("Where is today's P/E within its history?")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

Fields available in label templates: {ticker}, {label}, {x_value} (the date), {y_value} / {value} and {statistic}.

A specific date works too, with the date as a string. Several references can live in the same tag list:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(pe)
    .graph_box_whiskers(series=[
        {
            "ticker": "SPX",
            "label": "S&P 500",
            "tag": [
                {"x_values": "2020-03-23", "dot": {"color": "orange", "size": 40, "zorder": 8},
                 "tag": {"label": "{x_value:%b-%y}\n{y_value:.1f}x", "ubic_etq": (-30, 0), "fontsize": 7}},
                {"x_values": "last", "dot": {"color": "#B7331F", "size": 40, "zorder": 8},
                 "tag": {"label": "Today\n{y_value:.1f}x", "ubic_etq": (30, 0), "fontsize": 7}},
            ],
        },
    ])
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
)

docs.title: Label the statistics of the box
docs.text:
Use mode="statistic" (or simply give statistic) to annotate calculated values instead of observations. Available statistics: "low", "high" (the whisker ends), "mean", "median", "q1", "q3".

def stat_ref(statistic, text, offset):
    return {
        "statistic": statistic,
        "tag": {"label": text, "ubic_etq": offset, "fontsize": 6.5, "font_color": "#333333"},
    }

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(pe)
    .graph_box_whiskers(series=[
        {
            "ticker": ticker,
            "tag": [
                stat_ref("high", "{y_value:.1f}", (0, 5)),
                stat_ref("median", "{y_value:.1f}", (26, 0)),
                stat_ref("low", "{y_value:.1f}", (0, -9)),
            ],
        }
        for ticker in pe.columns
    ])
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
)

q1 and q3

The quartiles are calculated from the data and the whiskers follow whis. If you change whis, the low / high statistics follow the same rule as the drawn whiskers.

docs.title: Mean line, notch and horizontal boxes
docs.text:
box_config is passed to Axes.boxplot; the most useful keys are:

Key Default Description whis (0, 100) Whisker rule: percentiles tuple or a multiple of the IQR. showfliers False Draw outliers. showmeans, meanline False Show the mean (as a marker or, with meanline, as a line). widths 0.6 Width of the boxes. notch False Notched boxes. vert True False = horizontal boxes. 

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(pe)
    .graph_box_whiskers(
        box_config={"vert": False, "showmeans": True, "meanline": True, "widths": 0.5},
        mean_style={"color": "#B7331F", "linestyle": "--", "linewidth": 1.0},
        series=[
            {"ticker": "SPX", "label": "S&P 500"},
            {"ticker": "NDX", "label": "Nasdaq 100"},
            {"ticker": "SX5E", "label": "Euro Stoxx 50"},
            {"ticker": "MXEF", "label": "MSCI EM"},
        ],
    )
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .vertical_guides()
)

docs.title: Styling the parts of the box
docs.text:
Parameter What it styles Default box_style Box border {"color": "#6E6E6E", "linewidth": 0.5} median_style Median line {"color": "#222222", "linewidth": 1.5} whisker_style Whiskers {"color": "#6E6E6E", "linewidth": 0.5} cap_style Whisker caps {"color": "#6E6E6E", "linewidth": 0.5} flier_style Outliers gray circles mean_style Mean marker / line {"color": "#404040", "linewidth": 0.5, "linestyle": "--"} box_face_alpha Opacity of the box fill 0.50

Each dictionary is merged over the default (you only pass what you want to change).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description series all numeric columns List of dicts / BoxSeriesConfig: ticker, label, color, tag. df_index 0 DataFrame of the object to use. box_config see above Keyword arguments of Axes.boxplot. box_style, median_style, whisker_style, cap_style, flier_style, mean_style see above Matplotlib property dictionaries. box_face_alpha 0.50 Fill opacity. x_axis None Category labels: fontsize, rotation, ha, label_color, tick_labels, tick_label_map. See Axes.

Full signature: API reference.

docs.title: Typical use cases
docs.text:
• Historical P/E, EV/EBITDA or P/B ratios (with the last value highlighted).
  • Historical yields and credit spreads.
  • Margin, volatility or drawdown distributions.
  • Relative valuation across indices, sectors or countries.

docs.title: Distribution chart: graph_dist
docs.text:
graph_dist() draws a histogram of one or more series and can overlay probability curves: curves of a known distribution (you provide the parameters) and curves fitted to the data (parameters estimated from it, or a kernel density estimate). It can also highlight references on the distribution: the last observation, a specific date, a literal value (e.g. a VaR) or a statistic (mean, median, percentiles).

Typical question it answers: "Is today's return / spread / multiple unusual compared with its own history?"

docs.title: Expected DataFrame
docs.text:
Each column is a series, and its values form the distribution. The index is only used to find observations ("last", a date) when you want to highlight them.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

dates = pd.bdate_range("2019-01-02", periods=1500)
returns = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Portfolio": rng.standard_t(5, len(dates)) * 0.0045 + 0.0004,
        "Benchmark": rng.standard_t(5, len(dates)) * 0.0060 + 0.0003,
    },
    index=dates,
)


returns.describe().round(4).loc[["count", "mean", "std", "min", "max"]]
Output

       Portfolio  Benchmark
count  1500.0000  1500.0000
mean      0.0001     0.0003
std       0.0059     0.0081
min      -0.0487    -0.0340
max       0.0292     0.0513

docs.title: Basic histogram
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(series=[{"ticker": "Portfolio", "label": "Portfolio daily returns"}], bins=40)
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .add_title("Distribution of daily returns")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

By default the y-axis is a density (area = 1). With x_axis={"fmt": ".1%"} the values of the distribution axis (the x-axis) are shown as percentages, and tick_values chooses the tick positions.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(
        series=[{"ticker": "Portfolio"}],
        bins=40,
        x_axis={"fmt": ".1%", "tick_values": [-0.02, -0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02]},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
)

tick_step on a distribution axis

On a distribution axis tick_step is expressed in axis units and must be an integer (e.g. tick_step=10 for a spread in basis points). For fractional steps, as with returns, list the ticks in tick_values.

docs.title: Count or probability instead of density
docs.text:
stat accepts "density" (default), "count" or "probability" (the bar heights sum to 1). Curves are rescaled to the same unit.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(series=[{"ticker": "Portfolio"}], bins=30, stat="count", fit="norm")
    .config_yaxis(fmt=",.0f")
    .add_title("Number of days in each return bucket")
)

docs.title: Compare two distributions
docs.text:
With several series, common_bins=True (default) uses the same bin edges so the bars are comparable. The histogram transparency is hist_alpha (default 0.45).

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(
        series=[
            {"ticker": "Portfolio", "color": "#12275A"},
            {"ticker": "Benchmark", "color": "#B7331F"},
        ],
        bins=50,
        x_range=(-0.03, 0.03),
        x_axis={"fmt": ".0%"},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("Portfolio vs benchmark")
)

x_range=(min, max) restricts the data used (values outside are ignored); either side can be None.

docs.title: Curves: fit and known
docs.text:
Argument Meaning Where parameters come from fit Curves estimated from each series ("norm", "t", "lognorm", ... any scipy.stats name, or "kde"). Estimated from the data. known Curves of a known distribution you specify. You provide params.

Both accept a name, a dictionary, a DistCurveConfig, or a list mixing them. Examples:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(
        series=[{"ticker": "Portfolio"}],
        bins=45,
        fit=[
            "norm",
            {"dist": "t", "color": "#2E7D32", "linestyle": "-.", "label_template": "t (df={df:.1f})"},
            {"dist": "kde", "fill": True, "color": "#B7331F", "label_template": "KDE"},
        ],
        x_axis={"fmt": ".1%", "tick_values": [-0.02, -0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02]},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("Fitted distributions")
)

A known curve is useful for the "what the model assumes" comparison, e.g. a normal with the target volatility of a mandate:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(
        series=[{"ticker": "Portfolio"}],
        bins=45,
        known={
            "dist": "norm",
            "params": {"loc": 0.0, "scale": 0.0045},
            "color": "#B7331F",
            "linestyle": "--",
            "label_template": "Target N(μ={mu:.1%}, σ={sigma:.2%})",
        },
        x_axis={"fmt": ".1%", "tick_values": [-0.02, -0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02]},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Curve options
docs.text:
Key Description dist scipy.stats name ("norm", "t", "lognorm"...) or "kde" (only in fit). In known it can also be a frozen scipy distribution or a callable pdf(x). params (known) dict ({"loc": 0, "scale": 1}) or tuple of positional parameters. Omitted = scipy defaults. fit_kwargs (fit) extra arguments of dist.fit, e.g. {"floc": 0}. bw_method (kde) bandwidth rule or factor. color, linewidth (lw), linestyle (ls), alpha, zorder Line style. label / label_template Fixed legend text, or a template with {series}, {ticker}, {dist}, {dist_key}, {kind}, {params}, {n}, every parameter by name ({loc}, {scale}, {df}...), {mu}, {sigma} and {bandwidth} (kde). legend False hides the curve from the legend. param_fmt, param_sep Format and separator used by {params} (defaults ".3g" and ", "). fill True or {"color", "alpha", "zorder", "hatch"}. line_kwargs Any extra Axes.plot argument.

The same curve can be written with the dataclass:

from helpers_ps.MtpltGraph.models import DistCurveConfig

fit=[DistCurveConfig("t", color="#2E7D32", linestyle="-."), DistCurveConfig("kde", fill=True)]

Default legend names are in Spanish

Fitted / theoretical curves get an automatic legend such as Normal ajustada (μ=..., σ=...) ({kind} is ajustada or teórica). Use label or label_template to write your own text.

One default for every series

fit and known set at function level apply to every series that does not define its own. Inside a series, fit=[] / known=[] disables them for that series only.

docs.title: Highlight references (VaR, last return, percentiles)
docs.text:
Each series accepts a tag list. Every item is a reference that can draw a vertical line, a text tag and a dot (show combines "line", "tag" and "dot", e.g. "line_tag", "line_tag_dot").

A reference is selected with one of three modes (inferred if omitted):

mode Key Meaning "observation" x_values The value the series takes at "last", "first" or any index label (a date). "value" value A literal number (or list) on the distribution axis, e.g. a VaR you computed. "statistic" statistic "mean", "median", "q1", "q3", "min", "max" or a percentile "p5", "p95" (any p<N>, 0-100). Accepts a list.

Template fields (template, legend_label): {ticker}, {label}, {x_value}, {value} ({y_value}), {statistic}, {percentile} (empirical rank 0-100), {zscore} and {density}. Default template: "{value:,.4g}\nP{percentile:.0f}".

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(
        series=[{
            "ticker": "Portfolio",
            "label": "Daily return",
            "color": "#12275A",
            "tag": [
                # last observation of the series, with its percentile
                {
                    "x_values": "last",
                    "show": "line_tag_dot",
                    "template": "Today\n{value:.2%} (P{percentile:.0f})",
                    "line": {"color": "#B7331F", "linewidth": 1.2},
                    "dot": {"color": "#B7331F", "size": 35},
                    "tag": {"font_color": "#B7331F", "fontsize": 7, "ubic_etq": (0, 20)},
                },
                # the 5th percentile (historical 95% VaR)
                {
                    "statistic": "p5",
                    "show": "line_tag",
                    "template": "VaR 95%\n{value:.2%}",
                    "line": {"color": "#555555", "linestyle": "--"},
                    "tag": {"fontsize": 7, "ubic_etq": (6, 55), "label_h_align": "left"},
                },
                # a literal value: the mandate's loss limit
                {
                    "value": -0.015,
                    "show": "line_tag",
                    "template": "Limit\n{value:.1%}",
                    "line": {"color": "#C9A227"},
                    "tag": {"fontsize": 7, "ubic_etq": (-6, 35), "label_h_align": "right"},
                },
            ],
        }],
        bins=45,
        x_axis={"fmt": ".1%", "tick_values": [-0.02, -0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02]},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .add_title("Is today unusual?")
)

Reference options:

Key Default Description mode, x_values, value, statistic inferred Selection (see above). show "line_tag" Combination of line, tag, dot. template, legend_label see above Text of the tag / legend entry. y_from "auto" Height used to anchor dots and tags: "hist" (bar height), "curve" (first curve) or "auto". line none extent ("curve" or "top"), color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha, zorder. tag none Arguments of tag(). dot none Arguments of dot().

docs.title: Only the curves
docs.text:
hist=False hides the histogram of a series (at least one curve is then required). It is a clean way to compare shapes:

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(returns)
    .graph_dist(
        series=[
            {"ticker": "Portfolio", "hist": False, "color": "#12275A"},
            {"ticker": "Benchmark", "hist": False, "color": "#B7331F"},
        ],
        fit=[{"dist": "kde", "fill": True, "label_template": "{series}"}],
        x_range=(-0.03, 0.03),
        x_axis={"fmt": ".0%"},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".0f")
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description series all numeric columns List of dicts / DistSeriesConfig: ticker, label, color, hist, known, fit, tag. df_index 0 DataFrame to use. bins "auto" Anything accepted by numpy.histogram_bin_edges: an integer, a rule ("auto", "fd") or explicit edges. stat "density" "density", "count" or "probability". common_bins True Same bin edges for all series. hist_alpha, hist_edgecolor, hist_linewidth 0.45, "white", 0.4 Bar style. hist_style None Extra Axes.hist arguments, e.g. {"histtype": "step"}. known, fit None Default curves for all series. curve_points 400 Resolution of the curves (>= 20). x_range None (min, max) of the data used. lw 1.6 Default width of curves. x_axis None Distribution-axis format: fmt, tick_step (integer, axis units), tick_values, tick_labels, fontsize, rotation, lim... plus fontweight, fontstyle, tick_color, spine_color, axis_label, axis_label_fontsize, axis_label_color when passed as a dictionary. bbg_format is not allowed.

Full signature: API reference.

docs.title: Line chart: parameters and series options
docs.text:
This page is the quick reference of graph_line(). For step-by-step examples see the Line chart notebook.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
dates = pd.bdate_range("2023-01-02", periods=520)
rets = rng.normal([0.0004, 0.0006, 0.0002], [0.009, 0.013, 0.004], size=(len(dates), 3))
prices = pd.DataFrame(
    100 * np.exp(rets.cumsum(axis=0)),
    index=dates,
    columns=["SPX", "NDX", "AGG"],
)

docs.title: Method parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description series all columns List of dictionaries / LineSeriesConfig (see below). df_index 0 DataFrame of the object to use. lw 1.6 Default line width. A series can override it with its own lw. x_axis None X-axis settings: Axes.

docs.title: Series keys
docs.text:
Key Default Description ticker required Column of the DataFrame. Each column may be used only once. label the ticker Name in the legend and in tag templates ({label}). color next palette color Any Matplotlib color ("#12275A", "red"). axis_side "left" "left" or "right": series of the right side share a secondary y-axis. lw method lw Line width of this series. linestyle "-" "-", "--", "-.", ":" (or solid, dashed, dashdot, dotted) or a dash tuple such as (0, (5, 2)). tags None List of annotations: Annotations. 

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(prices)
    .graph_line(
        series=[
            {"ticker": "SPX", "label": "Solid, thick", "color": "#12275A", "lw": 2.4},
            {"ticker": "NDX", "label": "Dashed", "color": "#B7331F", "linestyle": "--"},
            {"ticker": "AGG", "label": "Dotted (right axis)", "color": "#3075DB", "linestyle": ":", "axis_side": "right", "lw": 2},
        ],
        lw=1.4,
    )
    .add_legend()
)

docs.title: Index types
docs.text:
Index Behavior DatetimeIndex Time axis (see bbg_format to remove non-trading gaps). Numeric Numeric axis (points are placed at their numeric value): strikes, durations or any x vs y curve. Text Categorical axis (equally spaced positions 0, 1, 2...), e.g. maturity labels.

A yield curve is a line chart with a text (categorical) index; tick_step=1 prints every maturity:

curve = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Today": [4.3, 4.2, 4.0, 3.9, 4.1, 4.4], "Last year": [5.3, 5.2, 4.9, 4.6, 4.5, 4.7]},
    index=["3M", "1Y", "2Y", "5Y", "10Y", "30Y"],   # maturities as text
)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(curve)
    .graph_line(
        series=[{"ticker": "Today", "color": "#12275A", "lw": 2.2}, {"ticker": "Last year", "color": "#B7331F", "linestyle": "--"}],
        x_axis={"tick_step": 1},
    )
    .config_yaxis(fmt=".1f")
    .horizontal_guides(mostrar_cero=False)
    .add_legend()
    .add_title("US Treasury yield curve")
)

docs.title: Pie chart: graph_pie
docs.text: graph_pie() draws a pie or donut chart from one column of values. The index holds the categories (slice names) and the column holds the weights. Use it for a snapshot in time: asset allocation, sector, country, currency or rating distribution.

docs.title: Expected DataFrame
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
import helpers_ps as hp

hp.set_graph_theme()

weights = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Weight": [0.42, 0.31, 0.15, 0.08, 0.04]},
    index=["US equity", "Global bonds", "EM equity", "Gold", "Cash"],
)


weights
Output

              Weight
US equity       0.42
Global bonds    0.31
EM equity       0.15
Gold            0.08
Cash            0.04
  • The index values are the categories; it must be unique.
  • Values cannot be negative and at least one must be greater than zero.
  • If the DataFrame has one column, ticker can be omitted. With several columns, pass ticker="ColumnName".

A time series? Take a snapshot first

graph_pie() does not select dates. To chart the weights at the last date of a wide DataFrame (index = dates, one column per asset), transpose the row you want:

snapshot = wide_df.iloc[[-1]].T      # index = assets, one column = last date
hp.GraphMtplt(snapshot).graph_pie()

docs.title: Basic pie
docs.text:
g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(weights)
    .graph_pie()
    .add_title("Strategic allocation")
    .add_source("Source: simulated data")
)

By default the first slice starts at 12 o'clock and the others follow clockwise (startangle=90, counterclock=False) and percentages are printed with one decimal (autopct="%1.1f%%").

docs.title: Donut
docs.text:
donut_width (0-1) is the width of the ring as a fraction of the radius: 1 is a full pie, smaller values give a thinner ring.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(weights)
    .graph_pie(donut_width=0.45, sort_values=True, pctdistance=0.78, autopct="%1.0f%%")
    .add_title("Donut, sorted from largest to smallest")
)

docs.title: Labels, colors and exploded slices
docs.text:
labels, colors and explode accept a list (same order as the index) or a dictionary keyed by category. A single color string paints every slice; a short list of colors repeats cyclically.

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt(weights)
    .graph_pie(
        labels={"US equity": "US", "Global bonds": "Bonds", "EM equity": "EM"},   # missing keys keep the index name
        colors={"US equity": "#12275A", "Global bonds": "#3075DB", "EM equity": "#B7331F"},
        explode={"EM equity": 0.08},
        startangle=60,
        label_color="#333333",
    )
)

docs.title: Hide percentages or category names
docs.text:
autopct=None removes the percentages and labeldistance=None removes the category names from the chart. Names are then usually shown in a legend. Pie slices do not feed the automatic legend, so register one marker per category with add_legend_point() and then call add_legend():

palette = {
    "US equity": "#12275A",
    "Global bonds": "#3075DB",
    "EM equity": "#B7331F",
    "Gold": "#C9A227",
    "Cash": "#7F7F7F",
}

g = hp.GraphMtplt(weights).graph_pie(
    colors=palette,
    autopct=None,
    labeldistance=None,
    donut_width=0.4,
)

for name, color in palette.items():
    g.add_legend_point(label=name, color=color, marker="s", markersize=8)

g.add_legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5))

docs.title: Several pies in one figure
docs.text:
Use plot() to create the grid and axis() to select each panel. Every panel can use a different DataFrame of the list:

current = weights
target = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Weight": [0.35, 0.35, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05]},
    index=weights.index,
)

g = (
    hp.GraphMtplt([current, target])
    .plot(ncols=2, figsize=(8, 4))
    .add_title("Current vs target allocation")
    .axis(0).graph_pie(df_index=0, donut_width=0.5).add_plot_title("Current")
    .axis(1).graph_pie(df_index=1, donut_width=0.5).add_plot_title("Target")
)

Call add_title() before add_plot_title()

add_title() clears the title of the active axis. If you call it after add_plot_title(), the title of that panel disappears.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description ticker None Column to plot. Optional when the DataFrame has one column. df_index 0 DataFrame of the object to use. labels index names List or dict of display names. colors palette List, dict or a single color. explode None Offset of slices: number, list or dict (non-negative). donut_width None None = full pie; 0 < w <= 1 = donut. startangle 90 Angle of the first slice. counterclock False Draw slices counterclockwise. autopct "%1.1f%%" Percentage format. None hides them. A callable is accepted. pctdistance 0.72 Radial position of the percentages (0 center, 1 edge). labeldistance 1.05 Radial position of the names. None hides them. normalize True Rescale values so they sum to 100%. With False, values that sum less than 1 draw a partial pie. sort_values False Sort slices from largest to smallest. textprops, wedgeprops None Raw Matplotlib dictionaries (wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white"}). label_color, autopct_color, autopct_fontweight "black", "white", "bold" Text colors / weight. text_edge_color, text_edge_width None, 0.0 Outline around the text to improve readability.
